docs.title: ChemMatData
docs.text:
The chem_mat_data package provides easy access to a large range of property prediction datasets from Chemistry and Material Science. The aim of this package is to provide the datasets in a unified format suitable to machine learning applications and specifically to train graph neural networks (GNNs).

Specifically, chem_mat_data addresses these aims by providing simple, single-line command line (CLI) and programming (API) interfaces to download datasets either in raw or in processed (graph) format.

Features:

  • 🐍 Easily installable via pip
  • 📦 Instant access to a collection of datasets across the domains of chemistry and material science
  • 🤖 Direct support of popular graph deep learning libraries like Torch/PyG and Jax/Jraph
  • 🤝 Large python version compatibility
  • ⌨️ Comprehensive command line interface (CLI)

docs.title: Loading Datasets
docs.text:
In chem_mat_data, each dataset is provided in a raw and a processed/graph format.

The raw format resembles the format in which the dataset was originally published in and is usually more compressed and therefore more storage- and bandwidth-efficient to work with. For molecular datasets, this raw format usually simply consists of a list of SMILES strings that represents different molecules and their corresponding target value annotations. Since it is more data efficient, this format is recommended when working with machine learning methods that do not require the full graph representation, such as methods based on molecular fingerprints.

The processed/graph format contains the already pre-processed full graph information for each molecule in the dataset. This format represents each molecule as a graph structure where all atoms are represented as graphs and all bonds as the corresponding edges. This format is recommended for machine learning methods based on graph neural networks (GNNs) since it removes the time-consuming graph pre-processing step.

docs.title: SMILES Dataset
docs.text:
For molecular property prediction tasks, the raw dataset format consists of a list of SMILES strings that represent the various molecules and their corresponding target value annotations.

A raw SMILES dataset can be loaded using the load_smiles_dataset function. This function will return a pandas.DataFrame object that contains a "smiles" column as well as various other columns that contain the target property annotations (whose names differe between the various datasets.)

import pandas as pd
from chem_mat_data import load_smiles_dataset

df: pd.DataFrame = load_smiles_dataset('clintox')
print(df.head())

docs.title: XYZ Datasets
docs.text:
Alternative to SMILES representations, some datasets are stored in the form of .XYZ files. The main difference of an XYZ dataset w.r.t. to a SMILES dataset is that the SMILES dataset contains the graph structure in the form of the bond information and the XYZ dataset contains additional geometry information in the form of atom coordinates.

A raw XYZ dataset can be loaded using the load_xyz_dataset function. This function will return a pandas.DataFrame object that most importantly contains the "mol" column as well as various other columns that contain the target property annotations or other additional values.

import pandas as pd
from chem_mat_data import load_xyz_dataset

df: pd.DataFrame = load_xyz_dataset('qm9', parser_cls='qm9')
print(df.head())

Different XYZ File Formats

There exist slightly different format specifications for .xyz files which vary in how the include which information. The parser_cls parameter of the load_xyz_dataset function can be used to specify a distinct parser to be used to load the dataset in question. To find out which parser to use, one can use the cmdata info command for the dataset in question.

docs.title: Loading Processed Datasets
docs.text:
The processed/graph format of a dataset can be loaded with the load_graph_dataset function. This function will return a list of dict objects which contain various key value pairs that describe the full graph structure of the molecule. For more information on the structure of these graph representations visis the Graph Representation documentation.

from rich.pretty import pprint
from chem_mat_data import load_graph_dataset

graphs: list[dict] = load_graph_dataset('clintox')
print(f'loaded {len(graphs)} graphs')
example_graph = graphs[0]
pprint(example_graph)

docs.title: Streaming Datasets
docs.text: The chem_mat_data package provides an alternative approach to loading datasets through streaming datasets which load data lazily on-demand rather than loading entire datasets into memory at once. This approach is particularly beneficial when working with large datasets or in memory-constrained environments.

docs.title: Motivation
docs.text:
While the pre-processed graph datasets (see Loading Datasets) offer convenience by providing ready-to-use graph representations, they require loading the entire dataset into memory. For large datasets with hundreds of thousands of molecules, this can consume significant RAM and may not be feasible on consumer hardware or in shared computing environments.

Streaming datasets address these challenges through several key advantages:

Low Memory Footprint: Only the data currently being processed needs to be in memory. A streaming dataset can process arbitrarily large datasets - even those with millions of molecules - on hardware with limited RAM. This is because molecules are loaded and processed one at a time (or in small batches) rather than loading the entire dataset upfront.

Reduced Download Size: The streaming GraphDataset is based on compressed raw representations (SMILES strings or XYZ files) rather than pre-computed graph structures. These raw formats are significantly more compact than full graph representations, resulting in smaller file downloads and reduced bandwidth usage.

Flexible Processing: Since molecules are converted from raw representations to graphs on-the-fly, you can easily apply custom featurization by providing your own processing class. This eliminates the need to download multiple versions of the same dataset with different feature encodings.

Immediate Training: With streaming datasets, model training can begin immediately as data is loaded and processed in the background. There is no waiting period for the entire dataset to be loaded into memory before training starts.

Support for Multiple Formats: Streaming datasets work with both SMILES-based datasets (for connectivity only) and XYZ-based datasets (with 3D geometry), providing flexibility for different types of molecular modeling tasks.

These benefits make streaming datasets the recommended approach for working with large-scale datasets, experimenting with custom features, or training in resource-constrained environments.

docs.title: SmilesDataset
docs.text:
The SmilesDataset class provides streaming access to raw molecular datasets in SMILES format. It reads the CSV file containing SMILES strings and target properties line-by-line, yielding one molecule at a time without loading the entire dataset into memory.

This is the most memory-efficient way to work with molecular datasets and is particularly useful when you need access to the raw SMILES representations, for example when working with molecular fingerprints or other SMILES-based machine learning methods.

from chem_mat_data.dataset import SmilesDataset

# Create streaming dataset
dataset = SmilesDataset(
    dataset='aqsoldb',
    smiles_column='smiles',
    target_columns=['Solubility']
)

# Iterate through molecules one at a time
for smiles, properties in dataset:
    print(f"SMILES: {smiles}")
    print(f"Properties: {properties}")
    break  # Just show first example

The SmilesDataset automatically downloads and caches the raw CSV file if it doesn't exist locally. Each iteration yields a tuple of (smiles_string, properties_array) where the properties are returned as a numpy array.

docs.title: XyzDataset
docs.text:
The XyzDataset class provides streaming access to molecular datasets in XYZ format with 3D coordinate information. Unlike SMILES datasets which only contain molecular connectivity, XYZ datasets include the full 3D geometry of molecules - making them essential for tasks that require spatial information such as conformer generation, force field training, or 3D-QSAR methods.

XYZ datasets are stored as "xyz_bundle" folders containing individual .xyz files (one per molecule) and an optional meta.csv file with target properties and metadata. The dataset streams through these files one at a time, yielding molecular geometry and properties without loading the entire dataset into memory.

from chem_mat_data.dataset import XyzDataset

# Create streaming XYZ dataset
dataset = XyzDataset(
    dataset='qm9',
    parser_cls='qm9',  # Specify parser for QM9 format
    target_columns=['U0', 'U', 'H']
)

# Iterate through molecules one at a time
for xyz_data, properties in dataset:
    print(f"Atoms: {xyz_data['num_atoms']}")
    print(f"Positions shape: {xyz_data['positions'].shape}")  # (N, 3)
    print(f"Atomic numbers: {xyz_data['atomic_numbers']}")
    print(f"Properties: {properties}")
    break  # Just show first example

The XyzDataset automatically downloads and caches the xyz_bundle folder if it doesn't exist locally. Each iteration yields a tuple of (xyz_data, properties_array) where:

  • xyz_data is a dictionary containing:
    • positions: numpy array of shape (N, 3) with 3D atomic coordinates
    • atomic_numbers: numpy array of shape (N,) with atomic numbers
    • symbols: numpy array of shape (N,) with atom symbols (e.g., 'C', 'O', 'N')
    • num_atoms: integer count of atoms in the molecule
  • properties is a numpy array with target values

XYZ Format Variations

Different datasets use slightly different XYZ file formats to encode additional information. The parser_cls parameter specifies which parser to use when loading a specific dataset. Use cmdata info <dataset-name> to check which parser is required for a particular dataset. Common parsers include 'default', 'qm9', and 'hopv15'.

docs.title: GraphDataset
docs.text:
The GraphDataset class extends the streaming approach to provide on-the-fly conversion from raw molecular representations (SMILES strings or XYZ structures) to graph dict representations. Each molecule is processed into the same graph dict format used by the pre-processed datasets (see Graph Representation), but the processing happens as you iterate through the dataset rather than being pre-computed.

GraphDataset automatically detects whether to load data as a SmilesDataset or XyzDataset based on what's available for the specified dataset. This means you can use the same code for both SMILES-based and XYZ-based datasets, and the appropriate loader will be selected automatically.

docs.title: Sequential Processing
docs.text:
By default, or when setting num_workers=0, the GraphDataset operates in sequential mode. This processes one molecule at a time in a truly streaming manner with minimal memory overhead:

from rich.pretty import pprint
from chem_mat_data.dataset import GraphDataset

# Create streaming graph dataset from SMILES (sequential mode)
dataset = GraphDataset(
    dataset='aqsoldb',
    num_workers=0,  # Sequential processing
    smiles_column='smiles',
    target_columns=['Solubility']
)

# Iterate through graphs one at a time
for graph in dataset:
    pprint(graph)
    break  # Just show first example

Sequential processing is optimal for typical molecular datasets where RDKit graph generation is relatively fast (around 0.5ms per molecule). The simplicity of sequential processing avoids the overhead of multiprocessing coordination, making it the fastest option for most use cases.

docs.title: Working with XYZ Datasets
docs.text:
GraphDataset works seamlessly with XYZ-based datasets, automatically detecting and using XyzDataset when appropriate. This is particularly useful for datasets like QM9 that provide 3D geometries:

from chem_mat_data.dataset import GraphDataset

# Create streaming graph dataset from XYZ data
# GraphDataset automatically detects this is an XYZ dataset
dataset = GraphDataset(
    dataset='qm9',
    parser_cls='qm9',  # Required for XYZ datasets
    target_columns=['U0', 'U', 'H'],
    num_workers=0
)

# Iterate through graphs generated from 3D structures
for graph in dataset:
    # Same graph dict format as SMILES-based datasets
    print(f"Nodes: {len(graph['node_indices'])}")
    print(f"Node features shape: {graph['node_attributes'].shape}")
    break

The automatic detection follows a simple rule: it first tries to load as a SmilesDataset (checking for .csv file), and if that fails, it attempts to load as an XyzDataset (checking for .xyz_bundle folder). This transparent handling means you don't need to explicitly specify the dataset type.

docs.title: Parallel Processing
docs.text:
For complex molecules or datasets where processing time per molecule is significant, the GraphDataset supports parallel processing using multiple worker processes:

from chem_mat_data.dataset import GraphDataset

# Create streaming graph dataset with parallel processing
dataset = GraphDataset(
    dataset='aqsoldb',
    num_workers=4,      # Use 4 parallel worker processes
    buffer_size=100,    # Number of molecules to queue ahead
    smiles_column='smiles',
    target_columns=['Solubility']
)

# Iterate through graphs with parallel processing
for graph in dataset:
    # Graphs are processed in parallel while maintaining order
    pass

The parallel mode uses Python's multiprocessing to bypass the Global Interpreter Lock (GIL), enabling true CPU parallelism. The dataset maintains the original molecule order even though workers may complete processing at different rates. This is achieved through an internal priority queue that reorders results before yielding them.

When to Use Parallel Mode

Parallel processing introduces overhead from process coordination, queue operations, and data serialization. For typical small molecules, sequential mode is actually faster. Use parallel mode when:

  • Processing complex molecules (e.g., large polymers, proteins)
  • Using custom processing classes with CPU-intensive computations
  • Working with datasets where processing time exceeds 2ms per molecule
  • You have 4 or more CPU cores available for better amortization of overhead

docs.title: Custom Processing
docs.text:
The GraphDataset accepts a custom processing_class parameter to define your own featurization. This is particularly powerful for streaming datasets since you can experiment with different feature encodings without re-downloading the dataset:

from chem_mat_data.dataset import GraphDataset
from chem_mat_data.processing import MoleculeProcessing

# Use custom processing class (see Custom Pre-Processing docs)
class CustomProcessing(MoleculeProcessing):
    # Define custom node/edge attributes here
    pass

dataset = GraphDataset(
    dataset='aqsoldb',
    processing_class=CustomProcessing,
    num_workers=0
)

for graph in dataset:
    # Graphs use your custom feature encoding
    pass

For details on creating custom processing classes, see Custom Pre-Processing.

docs.title: ShuffleDataset
docs.text: Machine learning training typically requires data to be shuffled to prevent the model from learning spurious patterns based on data ordering. The ShuffleDataset wrapper provides approximate shuffling of streaming datasets using a shuffle buffer algorithm.

docs.title: How Shuffle Buffering Works
docs.text: The shuffle buffer algorithm provides randomization without loading the entire dataset into memory by maintaining a fixed-size buffer from which items are randomly selected and yielded, with each yielded item being replaced by the next item from the stream. The buffer size controls the trade-off between shuffling quality and memory usage - larger buffers provide better global shuffling (with buffer_size >= dataset_size giving perfect shuffling), while smaller buffers provide approximate shuffling with lower memory consumption. For most machine learning applications, a buffer size of 5,000-10,000 provides good shuffling quality while maintaining reasonable memory usage.

docs.title: Usage in Training
docs.text:
The ShuffleDataset is particularly useful for training graph neural networks where shuffled mini-batches are required:

from chem_mat_data.dataset import GraphDataset, ShuffleDataset

# Create base streaming dataset
base_dataset = GraphDataset(
    dataset='aqsoldb',
    num_workers=4
)

# Wrap with shuffle buffer
shuffled_dataset = ShuffleDataset(
    dataset=base_dataset,
    buffer_size=5000,  # Shuffle buffer of 5000 molecules
    seed=42            # Fixed seed for reproducibility
)

# Training loop
num_epochs = 10
for epoch in range(num_epochs):
    for graph in shuffled_dataset:
        # Each epoch iterates through all molecules in shuffled order
        # With same seed, each epoch uses identical shuffle order
        train_step(graph)

Reproducibility

Setting a fixed seed ensures that each iteration through the ShuffleDataset produces the same shuffle order. This is important for reproducible machine learning experiments. If seed=None, each iteration will produce a different random shuffle.

docs.title: Integration with Deep Learning Frameworks
docs.text:
While the streaming datasets are framework-agnostic, they work seamlessly with PyTorch DataLoaders and similar abstractions:

from chem_mat_data.dataset import GraphDataset, ShuffleDataset
from chem_mat_data.graph import graph_dict_to_pyg

# Create shuffled streaming dataset
dataset = ShuffleDataset(
    GraphDataset(dataset='aqsoldb', num_workers=4),
    buffer_size=5000,
    seed=42
)

# Training loop with on-the-fly conversion to PyG format
for graph_dict in dataset:
    # Convert to PyTorch Geometric format
    pyg_graph = graph_dict_to_pyg(graph_dict)

    # Use with your GNN model
    output = model(pyg_graph)
    loss = criterion(output, target)
    # ...

For details on converting graph dicts to framework-specific formats, see Graph Representation.

docs.title: When to Use Streaming Datasets
docs.text:
Streaming datasets are recommended when:

  • Large Datasets: Working with datasets containing more than 100,000 molecules where memory consumption is a concern
  • Limited Hardware: Training on consumer hardware or shared infrastructure with limited RAM
  • Custom Features: Experimenting with different featurization approaches without re-downloading datasets
  • Immediate Prototyping: Quick iteration where you want to start training immediately without waiting for full dataset loading
  • 3D Geometry Data: Working with XYZ datasets that include spatial coordinates for conformer-dependent predictions

docs.title: When to Use Pre-Processed Datasets
docs.text:
Pre-processed datasets (loaded via load_graph_dataset) are better when:

  • Small Datasets: For datasets under 50,000 molecules that easily fit in memory
  • Multiple Epochs: Training for many epochs where the one-time loading cost is amortized
  • Random Access: Algorithms that require index-based access to specific molecules
  • Standardization: When consistent, pre-computed features across research groups are important

docs.title: Choosing Between SMILES and XYZ
docs.text:
The choice between SmilesDataset and XyzDataset depends on your modeling needs:

  • Use SMILES for:

    • 2D molecular property prediction (e.g., toxicity, solubility, bioactivity)
    • Graph-based methods where only connectivity matters
    • Maximum memory efficiency (SMILES strings are extremely compact)
    • Datasets without 3D structural information

  • Use XYZ for:

    • 3D molecular property prediction (e.g., binding energies, conformer stability)
    • Force field development and quantum chemistry applications
    • Methods that require spatial information (e.g., 3D-QSAR, pharmacophore modeling)
    • Datasets like QM9 that provide valuable geometric information

When using GraphDataset, you don't need to explicitly choose - it automatically detects which format is available for your dataset and uses the appropriate loader.

In practice, streaming datasets and pre-processed datasets are complementary approaches. The chem_mat_data package provides both options so you can choose the approach that best fits your specific use case and computational environment.

docs.title: ChEMBL and ShareAlike — how ChemMatData answered it
docs.text: Status: DECIDED, 2026-08-19, by the maintainer — option A, comply. The twelve ChEMBL-derived datasets are labelled CC-BY-SA-3.0 via a new license metadata field. See ADR 009. Attribution (§4 step 1) was completed 2026-08-18; labelling (§4 steps 2 and 4) on 2026-08-19. This file is kept as the evidence behind that decision. Written 2026-08-18. Not legal advice — this is research assembled so that a person can decide, with the evidence in one place instead of being re-derived every time.

docs.title: Why this file exists
docs.text:
The dataset-extraction run esnuel_mca (Ree et al., Chem. Sci. 2025, 10.1039/D4SC07297A) blocked at its licence gate on two grounds. The first is specific to that paper and is dealt with in ../.dataset_work/esnuel_mca/reviews/license.md.

The second is not specific to it at all: the molecules come from ChEMBL, and ChEMBL is CC BY-SA 3.0 — ShareAlike. The extraction skill's policy escalates ShareAlike to a human, correctly. But answering it for this one dataset would leave the same question to be re-answered on the next ChEMBL-derived paper, and there will be many: ChEMBL underlies a large share of med-chem ML data.

And the question is not hypothetical or forward-looking. ChemMatData already redistributes eight ChEMBL-derived datasets, none of which attributes ChEMBL. That was discovered while investigating this run, not by design.

So the decision to take is a project policy, and it has a retrospective half as well as a prospective one.

docs.title: 1. What ChEMBL's licence actually says
docs.text:
Verified against three independent current sources — this is not inferred from context.

ChEMBL interface documentation, "Data Licensing" (https://chembl.gitbook.io/chembl-interface-documentation/about):

"Access to the web interface of ChEMBL is made under the EBI's Terms of Use. The ChEMBL data is made available on a Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0 Unported License."

ChEMBL FAQ — this is the one that spells out propagation (https://chembl.gitbook.io/chembl-interface-documentation/frequently-asked-questions/general-questions):

"The ChEMBL database is licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0 Unported License. This allows use, redistribution and adaption of ChEMBL as long as appropriate attribution is given (e.g., cite the current ChEMBL paper) and ensure that any adaptations are redistributed under the same license."

The current release's own files — https://ftp.ebi.ac.uk/pub/databases/chembl/ChEMBLdb/latest/README:

"The data content in ChEMBL is licensed under a highly permissive Creative Commons license - specifically the "CC Attribution-ShareAlike 3.0 Unported license", see LICENSE file. The required attribution should contain the url of the ChEMBL resource, and also the release version, e.g.:

ChEMBL data is from http://www.ebi.ac.uk/chembl - the version of ChEMBL is chembl_37.

This should be visible on the entry portal for a web resource in which ChEMBL is integrated, or contained with the documentation for any further distribution."

No change of terms was found. Consistent from the 2009 licensing FAQ through chembl_37 today. No migration to CC-BY or CC0.

One near-miss, recorded so nobody trips on it. An August 2025 ChEMBL blog post releases a text-mined IUPAC-name file "under a CC0 license". That is SureChEMBL, a different resource and a single auxiliary file. It is not ChEMBL core and does not change anything here.

EMBL-EBI's umbrella terms neither add nor remove anything — they place "no additional restrictions … other than those provided by the original data owners", and resource-specific terms "prevail" (https://www.ebi.ac.uk/about/terms-of-use/, rev. 2024-02-05).

docs.title: Three things ShareAlike here is not
docs.text:
Worth stating plainly, because ShareAlike gets pattern-matched to NonCommercial and they are not the same animal:

  • It is not NonCommercial. ChEMBL has been explicit since 2012 that the SA condition does not preclude commercial use. Nothing here stops a company training on the data.
  • It is not a prohibition on redistribution. ChEMBL's own FAQ says the licence "allows use, redistribution and adaption". Redistribution is invited, on conditions.
  • It is not the CSD situation. The tmQMg-L / CSD entry in rejected_datasets.md rests on a rightsholder whose published position is that redistribution requires a signed agreement. ChEMBL's position is the opposite. These two cases should not be reasoned about together.

docs.title: 2. What ShareAlike actually obliges — read from the licence text
docs.text:
The load-bearing distinction is Adaptation vs Collection, and CC BY-SA 3.0 Unported defines both (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/legalcode.en):

Adaptation means a work based upon the Work … including in any form recognizably derived from the original, except that a work that constitutes a Collection will not be considered an Adaptation for the purpose of this License.

Collection means a collection of literary or artistic works … in which the Work is included in its entirety in unmodified form along with one or more other contributions, each constituting separate and independent works in themselves, which together are assembled into a collective whole.

§4(b), the ShareAlike clause, ends with the sentence that bounds how far the obligation travels:

"This Section 4(b) applies to the Adaptation as incorporated in a Collection, but this does not require the Collection apart from the Adaptation itself to be made subject to the terms of the Applicable License."

§4(a) says the same thing about the unmodified Work.

What that means concretely for this project. ShareAlike would attach to the individual ChEMBL-derived dataset. It would not reach:

  • the ChemMatData catalogue as a whole,
  • the other 38 datasets in it,
  • the chem_mat_data package source code.

So the worst case is per-dataset licensing, not a copyleft event that swallows the project. That is a materially smaller problem than "ShareAlike" sounds like at first reading, and it is the single most useful fact in this document.

docs.title: The genuine open questions in the licence text
docs.text:
Three, and they are why this is a judgement call rather than a lookup:

  1. Is a processed ChemMatData dataset an "Adaptation" or a "Collection"? A Collection requires the Work "in its entirety in unmodified form". A ChemMatData dataset is a filtered subset re-encoded as graphs — closer to an Adaptation. But the boundary is not crisp for data, and CC's definitions are written for literary and artistic works.

  2. Are the individual data points even protected? A SMILES string and a measured Ki are facts. Facts are not copyrightable. What copyright can subsist in is the selection and arrangement of the database. Whether extracting 50,000 structures takes a protected "substantial part" of that selection is exactly the kind of question that has no clean answer without a lawyer.

  3. CC BY-SA 3.0 Unported does not mention database rights at all. Checked directly against the legal code: zero occurrences of "database" and zero of "sui generis". The §3 grant is a copyright grant, and the "Work" definition reaches "a compilation of data to the extent it is protected as a copyrightable work". The EU/UK sui generis database right is a separate right that 3.0 Unported does not expressly license — CC only addressed this properly in the ported EU 3.0 licences and in 4.0. EMBL-EBI sits in that jurisdiction. This cuts both ways: the licence may not clearly grant database rights, and equally may not clearly impose ShareAlike on extractions that engage them.

None of these is resolvable by reading harder. They are why this needs a person.

docs.title: 3. What the project's exposure actually is today
docs.text:
Ten scripts in chem_mat_data/scripts/ are ChEMBL-derived. Eight are published in chem_mat_data/metadata.yml; two exist as scripts only.

Dataset Published Compounds ChEMBL release recorded ChEMBL in sources dud_e yes 400,040 chembl_09 added 2026-08-18 riniker_1 yes 168,326 chembl_14 † added 2026-08-18 riniker_1_filtered yes 105,294 chembl_14 † added 2026-08-18 bl_chembl_reg yes 52,484 chembl_25 added 2026-08-18 riniker_2 yes 20,922 not established added 2026-08-18 bl_chembl_cls yes 8,780 chembl_25 added 2026-08-18 lipophilicity yes 4,199 not established added 2026-08-18 dpp4 yes 3,933 not established added 2026-08-18 moleculeace script only — no — pparg_binding script only — no — esnuel_mca (this run) blocked ~47,921 no —

≈764,000 compounds, about 12% of the collection's 6.2 million.

Provenance is not in doubt for any of them — each script says so in its own docstring or description (dud_e: "extracted from ChEMBL09 database"; lipophilicity: "from the ChEMBL database"; dpp4: "was extract from ChEMBL with DPP-4 target"; riniker_2: "37 biological targets from ChEMBL"). lipophilicity even carries graph_chemblid per molecule.

As first found, none of the eight listed ChEMBL in sources and none carried a licence note. That gap was closed on 2026-08-18 — see §4 below.

† chembl_14 for the two riniker_1* datasets was not recorded anywhere in this project; it was recovered from the source publication (Riniker & Landrum, J. Cheminform. 5, 26 (2013), PMC3686626), which states: "This selection process was repeated with ChEMBL version 14 (Heikamp and Bajorath extracted the actives from ChEMBL version 9)." riniker_2 (Subset II) comes from a later paper and the benchmarking-platform README does not state a version, so it remains unestablished rather than assumed to be 14.

Note also that dud_e and bl_chembl_* do record their release version — so for those, ChEMBL's prescribed attribution string is writable today. For esnuel_mca it is not: the paper never says which ChEMBL release Bayer's 50k subset came from, so "the version of ChEMBL is chembl_NN" cannot be completed without asking the authors.

docs.title: 4. What compliance would concretely require
docs.text:
If the decision is to comply rather than to conclude SA does not attach, the work is small and mostly mechanical:

  1. Attribution — DONE 2026-08-18. Added to each affected dataset's sources and a notes entry: ChEMBL data is from http://www.ebi.ac.uk/chembl - the version of ChEMBL is chembl_NN, plus the ChEMBL paper (Mendez et al., Nucleic Acids Res. 2019, 47, D930–D940, 10.1093/nar/gky1075). Where the release is unknown, say so explicitly rather than omitting the line.
  2. A per-dataset licence field. metadata.yml has no licence key today. Adding one is independently worth doing — it is the natural place for this, and for the CC-BY attributions the extraction pipeline already collects and then drops.
  3. Mark that changes were made. §3(b) requires an Adaptation to "take reasonable steps to clearly label, demarcate or otherwise identify that changes were made". The descriptions largely do this already by describing the processing.
  4. State CC-BY-SA-3.0 on the ChEMBL-derived datasets if they are treated as Adaptations.
  5. Decide what this means for cmdata's users — arguably nothing more than that the dataset they downloaded carries a licence they can read.

Steps 1–3 are worth doing under any of the options below, including "SA does not attach": attribution is a scientific-credit obligation before it is a legal one, and ChEMBL asks for it in a specific form.

docs.title: What was actually done on 2026-08-18
docs.text:
Step 1 only. Steps 2, 4 and 5 are untouched, because they encode a licence decision that has not been taken — nothing here labels any dataset CC-BY-SA-3.0.

  • https://www.ebi.ac.uk/chembl/ added to sources for all eight datasets.
  • A notes entry added to all eight, naming ChEMBL as the source of the structures, stating that ChEMBL is licensed CC BY-SA 3.0, and citing Mendez et al.

The shipped credit is deliberately generic and names no release version — a maintainer decision on 2026-08-18, taken for uniformity across the eight. Note that this is technically incomplete against ChEMBL's own formula, which asks that the attribution "contain the url of the ChEMBL resource, and also the release version". The versions that were established are not lost: they are recorded in the exposure table above, and can be folded into the shipped notes at any time if the project later decides to comply to the letter. - The same text was written into both chem_mat_data/metadata.yml (so it is live now) and each dataset's METADATA dict in chem_mat_data/scripts/ (so that re-running cmmanage metadata collect regenerates it rather than dropping it). The two were then checked to be byte-identical. - create_graph_datasets__dpp4.py had no METADATA dict at all — its catalogue entry is hand-curated and a regeneration would have silently lost verbose, tags and sources. One was added mirroring the existing catalogue entry exactly.

Not done, and worth someone's attention separately: dpp4 also declares no DATASET_TYPE, so it would regenerate as regression while the catalogue records classification. That is a pre-existing bug unrelated to licensing and was left alone.

docs.title: 5. The decision — taken 2026-08-19: option A
docs.text:
The maintainer chose to comply: label the ChEMBL-derived datasets CC-BY-SA-3.0 and accept that the obligation propagates to downstream users. Recorded in ADR 009, which also documents the field shape and the three code paths that had to learn about it.

Option C (ask EMBL-EBI) remains worth doing — it would settle whether ShareAlike legally attaches at all, and option A is the conservative answer taken without that confirmation. Doing so could only relax the position, never tighten it.

The four positions as they were put, for the record:

A. Comply — treat ChEMBL-derived datasets as Adaptations under CC-BY-SA-3.0. Label them CC-BY-SA-3.0, add ChEMBL attribution with release versions where known. Cost: downstream users of those eight datasets inherit a reciprocal obligation, and the catalogue becomes licence-heterogeneous. Benefit: unambiguously correct, and matches what ChEMBL asks for. Under this option esnuel_mca can proceed, with the caveat that its release version is unknown.

B. Attribute but do not propagate — take the position that a ChemMatData dataset of computed properties keyed to structures is not an Adaptation of ChEMBL's selection, or that the underlying facts are unprotected. Add full attribution regardless. Cost: rests on a legal judgement the project would be making without counsel; should be written down as a deliberate position, not left implicit. Benefit: no obligation propagates to users; matches what the wider field does — DeepChem/MoleculeNet, TDC and OGB all redistribute ChEMBL-derived data under permissive licences.

C. Ask EMBL-EBI. They have a licensing contact and answer this kind of question. Cost: time. Benefit: the answer is authoritative, settles all eight existing datasets and every future one, and is quotable in this file forever.

D. Stop adding ChEMBL-derived datasets and decide separately what to do about the eight already published. Cost: excludes a large fraction of med-chem ML data. Probably only attractive if C comes back badly.

What was recommended at the time: C first, then A or B depending on the answer — and do steps 1–3 of §4 immediately regardless, because they are required under every option and cost an afternoon. C is cheap, and the difference between A and B is precisely the thing EMBL-EBI is placed to answer and this project is not.

Whatever is decided, record it in this file with the date and who decided, and add a line to rejected_datasets.md under "Checked and approved — do not re-litigate" so the extraction agent stops re-researching it.

docs.title: 6. Not in question
docs.text:
• ChEMBL permits redistribution. Nobody needs to establish that; the FAQ says so.
  • Commercial use is fine. SA is not NC.
  • The chem_mat_data package licence is unaffected. §4(b) does not reach the Collection, let alone the code.
  • The MCA/MAA values in esnuel_mca are not ChEMBL's. They are the authors' own r2SCAN-3c//GFN1-xTB computations. Only the smiles column is ChEMBL-derived. The same is true of most datasets in the table above — the structures are ChEMBL's, the measurements and computations are the papers'.

docs.title: 7. How to tell whether a new dataset is ChEMBL-derived
docs.text:
For the extraction agent, since this will keep coming up. ChEMBL provenance is usually one step removed and stated only in passing:

  • a CHEMBL\d+ identifier column, or target names like CHEMBL1862_Ki;
  • "drug-like subset", "bioactivity data", "curated from the literature" in a methods section, with ChEMBL named once in an acknowledgement rather than in the data statement — which is exactly how esnuel_mca states it;
  • benchmark lineage: MoleculeNet lipophilicity, MoleculeACE, the RDKit benchmarking platform, DUD-E actives and Briem–Lessel recreations are all ChEMBL underneath.

bace_cls / bace_reg were checked and are not flagged as ChEMBL-derived by their own scripts; they are literature-compiled. That was verified rather than assumed, and is recorded here so it is not re-checked.

docs.title: cache - Interacting with the Local File System Cache
docs.text:
The chem_mat_data package can be used to download various datasets from a remote file share server. To make sure that datasets only need to be actually downloaded once, the package uses a local file system cache. Whenever a dataset is downloaded for the first time, the corresponding files are placed in the cache and if the same dataset is requested again, it is simply copied from the cache rather than downloaded from the remote server.

The cmdata command line interface provides the cache command group to interact with this cache folder:

cmdata cache --help

docs.title: Viewing Cache Information
docs.text:
To view detailed information about the cache including its location, total size, and statistics, you can use the cache info command:

cmdata cache info

This will display comprehensive information about the cache directory, including the cache path, total size in MB or GB, the number of datasets stored, and the total number of files in the cache.

docs.title: Viewing the Cache Content
docs.text:
To view all the files that are currently stored in the cache, you can use the cache list command:

cmdata cache list

This will print a list view of all the files that are currently stored in the cache directory, divided by the raw and processed dataset files.

docs.title: Removing a Specific Dataset
docs.text:
To remove a specific dataset from the cache, you can use the cache remove command:

cmdata cache remove "dataset_name"

By default, this removes the .mpack (processed) version of the dataset. You can specify a different format using the --type option:

cmdata cache remove "dataset_name" --type csv

This command will remove only the specified dataset file from the cache, leaving all other cached datasets intact.

docs.title: Resetting the Cache
docs.text:
If you wich to reset the cache for some reason, you can use the cache clear command:

cmdata cache clear

This command will delete all the files in the cache folder.

docs.title: config - Interacting with the Local Config File
docs.text: When using the cmdata CLI, a local config.yml file is automatically created in the user's .config folder. This config file contains certain options that configure the behavior of the package.

docs.title: Viewing the Config File
docs.text:
To view the content of the current config file, you can use the config show command:

cmdata config show

docs.title: Edit the Config File
docs.text:
To conveniently edit this config file, you can use the config edit command:

cmdata config edit

This command will open the config file using the system's default text editor.

docs.title: download - Download Dataset
docs.text:
You can use the download command to download the datasets to the local file system by supplying the unique string identifier of the corresponding dataset (see List Available Datasets):

cmdata download "clintox"

This command will download the raw dataset files into the current working directory (CWD).

docs.title: Changing the Destination Path
docs.text:
You can change the destination directory for the download using the --path option:

cmdata download --path="/tmp" "clintox"

docs.title: Downloading the Graph Dataset
docs.text:
By default the command downloads the raw version of each dataset. You can supply --full flag to also download the processed/graph version of the dataset as well:

cmdata download --full "clintox"

This command will download the raw clintox.csv file and the clintox.mpack file. The processed dataset is stored in the MessagePack file format, which is essentially a binary version of the JSON format. When decoding this file with a programming language of choice, it will yield a list/sequence of graph dictionaries/objects as described in the Graph Representation documentation.

docs.title: info - Show Dataset Metadata
docs.text:
You can use the info command to view all the metadata associated with a specific dataset by supplying the unique string identifier of the corresponding dataset (see List Available Datasets)

cmdata info "clintox"

This will print a detail view as shown below. The detailed view about the dataset, for example, contains information about the number of elements it contains, the type of task it presents (regression/classification) and the description.

docs.title: list - List Available Datasets
docs.text:
You can use the list command to print a list view of all the datasets which are available on the remote file share server:

cmdata list

This will create a list view as shown below, where each dataset is identified by a unique string name (first column) and some additional information.

docs.title: Custom Pre-Processing of Graphs
docs.text:
The chem_mat_data package provides dataset in an already pre-processed graph format. This pre-processed graph format makes some opinionated choices about which kinds of node and edge features are inlcuded to represent information about each individual atom or bond in the molecular graph.

If this pre-defined format for some reason isn't sufficient for a given dataset, there exists the possibility to define a custom Processing class to construct a pre-processing pipeline that converts the SMILES representations into graph structures.

docs.title: Creating a MoleculeProcessing Subclass
docs.text:
To define a custom pre-processing structure, one can define a custom subclass of the MoleculeProcessing subclass and define the desired node and edge features by modifying the node_attributes and edge_attributes class properties. Both properties have to be dictionary objects that define the node and edge features by providing a callback function or class that derives the desired property from the corresponding rdkit.Atom or rdkit.Bond objects.

In the following example we can define a customized processing class which only encodes a subset of atom types and only includes the mass of the atom as an additional feature. For the edge attributes we only encode the difference between single and double bonds.

from chem_mat_data.processing import MoleculeProcessing
from chem_mat_data.processing import OneHotEncoder, chem_prop, list_identity

# Has to inherit from MoleculeProcessing!
class CustomProcessing(MoleculeProcessing):

    node_attribute_map = {

        'mass': {
            # "chem_prop" is a wrapper function which will call the given 
            # property method on the rdkit.Atom object - in this case the 
            # GetMass() method - and pass the output to the transformation 
            # function given as the second argument. "list_identity" means 
            # that the value is simply converted to a list as it is.
            # Therefore, this configuration will result in outputs such as 
            # [12.08], [9.88] etc. as parts of the overall feature vector.
            'callback': chem_prop('GetMass', list_identity),
            # Provide a human-readable description of what this section of 
            # the node feature vector represents.
            'description': 'The mass of the atom'
        },

        'symbol': {
            # "OneHotEncoder" is a special callable class that can be used 
            # to automatically define one-hot encodings. The object will 
            # accept the output of the given chem prop - in this case the 
            # GetSymbol action on the rdkit.Atom - and create an integer 
            # one-hot vector according to the provided list. In this case, 
            # the encoding will encode a carbon as [1, 0, 0, 0], 
            # a oxygen as [0, 1, 0, 0] etc.
            'callback': chem_prop('GetSymbol', OneHotEncoder(
                ['C', 'O', 'N', 'S'],
                add_unknown=False,
                dtype=str,
            )),
            'description': 'One hot encoding of the atom type',
            'is_type': True,
            'encodes_symbol': True,
        },
    }

    edge_attributes = {
        'type': {
            'callback': chem_prop()
        }
    }

docs.title: Applying the Custom Processing
docs.text:
After the custom processing class has been defined it can be used in the same manner as the orginal MoleculeProcessing class to convert the SMILES string representations of the dataset into the graph representation by using the process method.

from rich.pretty import pprint

processing = CustomProcessing()

graph: dict = processing.process('CCCC')
pprint(graph)

docs.title: Defining Custom Transformation Callbacks
docs.text:
As introduced in the previous example, the chem_prop wrapper can be used to cast the output of an rdkit.Atom or rdkit.Bond atom to some transformation callback which is then supposed to return a list that will become part of the final node/edge feature vector.

The most simple usage is the list_identity transformation which will simply wrap the output value in a list as it is. An alternative is to use the existing OneHotEncoder class to convert the output of a property getter method into an integer one-hot encoded vector.

Alternatively, it is also possible to define a completely custom callback to derive properties from the atom / bond objects directly. The callback functions simply have to accept a single positional argument entity: Atom | Bond. callback function has to return a list of numeric values which will be appended to the overall feature vector.

import rdkit.Chem as Chem
from rich.pretty import pprint
from typing import List
from chem_mat_data.processing import MoleculeProcessing

def custom_callback(atom: Chem.Atom) -> List[float]:

    # Mass multiplied with the charge
    return [atom.GetMass() * atom.GetCharge()]


class CustomCallbackProcessing(MoleculeProcessing):

    node_attributes = {
        'mass_times_charge': {
            'callback': custom_callback,
            'description': 'atom mass multiplied with the charge',
        }
    }


processing = CustomCallbackProcessing()
graph = processing.process('CCCC')
pprint(graph)

docs.title: dataset-extraction: what to fix next, ranked
docs.text: Scope: the skill at .claude/skills/dataset-extraction/, its machinery in chem_mat_data/agent/, and the agent command group in chem_mat_data/manage.py. All line numbers are against e39f0c4 on branch dataset-extraction-skill (worktree /tmp/claude-1000/-media-ssd2-Programming-chem-mat-data/202e8fa6-6fde-4211-8f71-ae295073d8a0/scratchpad/wt4). Run artifacts are /tmp/claude-1000/-media-ssd2-Programming-chem-mat-data/202e8fa6-6fde-4211-8f71-ae295073d8a0/scratchpad/sandbox-elanos/.dataset_work/enalos_bp/. Nothing below is fixed by e39f0c4, which changed documentation only.

docs.title: The structural conclusion
docs.text:
Every real defect either validation run found was found by a fresh subagent, and no gate found any of them. The verification subagent found four (a hook docstring that described behaviour the code did not have, an int(data.get('CID', -1)) that can never reach its default, undocumented CID-0 passthrough, and the .mpack/.csv row-order mismatch). The license subagent found a fabricated paper title with the wrong first author — outside its brief, the most valuable catch of run 2. The gates passed every version, including the one whose docstring lied.

That is not a gap the gates can close by getting stricter about the same things. It is a division of labour, and the code half of it is currently mis-specified. The gates check that declared facts are internally consistent with each other; almost every field they compare is one the agent wrote against another field the same agent wrote. Where a gate does have access to an independently-produced record, it does not read it: pycomex writes experiment_meta.json and a byte-exact experiment_code.py into every results directory, and grep -rn 'experiment_meta|experiment_code|has_error|st_mtime' chem_mat_data/agent/ returns nothing.

Two consequences drive the ranking:

  1. The cheapest wins are making the gates read records the agent did not author (experiment_meta.json), and making the subagents' findings survive (agent status and the manifest currently throw them away).
  2. The second structural conclusion is smaller but more urgent: the skill now contains instructions that the code does not implement, and two of them were added yesterday. e39f0c4 added cmmanage agent status <slug> # shows the recorded license at SKILL.md:342 and at license.md:167. agent_status_command (manage.py:1808-1857) prints the slug, the source URL, and the six stage lines. It does not print the license. That instruction exists to stop an override from deleting the evidence that justified escalating, and it cannot be followed. Documentation fixes that outrun the code are how this skill accumulates its worst defects, because an agent trusts them.

docs.title: Ranked
docs.text: Ranked by severity of the underlying problem divided by cost. Confidence is marked per item: verified = I reproduced it against the code in this session; likely = the mechanism is verified but the harm is projected; speculative = design not yet probed.

docs.title: 1. agent status is blind, and the newest commit tells the agent to depend on it
docs.text:
Confidence: verified. Cost: small (~30 lines + 4 doc lines).

Three defects in one code path.

  • agent status renders only stage symbols, blocker and notes. SKILL.md:342 and license.md:167 — both added by e39f0c4 — instruct the agent to read the recorded license back with it before merging a human_override. It shows no license at all. The documented safeguard against an override deleting upstream_database, upstream_terms_url, upstream_license and attribution is unperformable, leaving "retype from memory" as the only option.
  • manage.py:1918-1921 writes notes = f'{len(report.warnings)} warning(s)' and discards the text. The real manifest records notes: 1 warning(s) for prepare and for license. The license line is the one place in the whole run where the difference between "benign human override" and "the upstream forbids derivative works" matters, and the manifest does not record which it was.
  • manage.py:1911-1916 records report.errors[0].message and drops errors 2..n. Blocked runs are exactly the ones resumed cold in a new session.

Change. (a) Print the license record in agent status — identifier, evidence URL, upstream_database/upstream_license when named, override decision and reason — plus the recorded warning and blocker text under each stage line. This makes SKILL.md:342 true. (b) Add warnings: List[str] and blockers: List[str] to StageState alongside notes (not replacing it — mark() writes notes='invalidated by a re-run of the …' at manifest.py:357, and tests/test_agent_pipeline.py:114 asserts on it), populate from report.warnings / report.errors. (c) Set allow_unicode=True on yaml.dump at manifest.py:298 in the same commit, or the first warning quoting a °C target description writes \xB0C into the manifest. (d) Add three lines to SKILL.md: --no-record and --strict exist (manage.py:1867-1877), neither appears anywhere under .claude/skills/.

Risk. agent status currently renders blocker or notes as an either/or (manage.py:1846-1849); a third field needs that branch restructured or a stale stage will swallow its warnings.

Note. This closes known-outstanding item 3 outright, and the briefing's framing of that item is wrong: --no-record already gives a read-only gate re-run. I confirmed all six gates re-run in-process against the real manifest with the file md5 unchanged. It is undocumented, not absent.

docs.title: 2. An approved license override waives every check, including the one added because of run 1
docs.text:
Confidence: verified. Cost: small (one function restructure + 3 lines).

gates.py:388-409 returns from gate_license inside the override branch, before the identifier, redistribution, attribution, upstream-database and host-divergence checks at 411-495. Probed against the real module:

  • {'evidence_url': ..., 'human_override': {'decision':'approved','reason':'looks fine to me'}} → ok=True, one warning reading license None approved by human override.
  • The real enalos_bp manifest with the override removed produces two ERRORs: redistribution is 'allowed by the data record itself …; the upstream … forbids distributing or preparing derivative works' and upstream database "US EPA EPI Suite …" is under "No open license…" which is not permissive. With the override, all of that collapses to the single green line license 'CC-BY-4.0' approved by human override. The gate report actively misrepresents the situation rather than merely under-describing it.

Separately, gates.py:768 guards the final re-check on the override's presence: if not override and not is_permissive(...). Loading the real manifest and mutating it: flipping the decision to rejected → gate_verification ok=True, zero issues; setting decision: maybe → ok=True; deleting evidence_url → ok=True; changing the identifier to CC-BY-NC-4.0 → ok=True. The recheck cannot detect any change to the license record while an override key is present. SKILL.md stage 6 tells the reader this gate confirms "the license conclusion still holds".

Also: SKILL.md:318-319's bolded "upstream_database is not optional — omitting the key fails the gate" is false whenever an override exists.

Change. (a) Restructure gate_license to collect all issues first, then, when an approved override is present, downgrade each ERROR to a WARNING prefixed verbatim (waived by human override: upstream database "US EPA EPI Suite" is under …), followed by the reason. Keep the verdict ok=True — the override is the designed escape hatch and test_human_override_still_wins_over_upstream names that intent. Both existing override tests assert only .ok and survive. Fix the license None rendering to no license identified in the same edit. (b) Replace gates.py:765-772 with for issue in gate_license(manifest).issues: report.add(issue.level, issue.message). Three lines, and it subsumes rejected / garbage-decision / deleted-evidence / changed-identifier / newly-restrictive-upstream at once.

Risk. Waived warnings multiply the license stage's warning count (the real run goes 1 → 3), so agent gate license --strict would then fail every overridden license. Decide deliberately whether waived warnings are exempt from --strict. Re-running gate_license inside gate_verification means any license ERROR now blocks the final gate — correct, but it will block runs whose license record was edited after stage 3 passed.

Do not require an identifier before an override can be approved (license.md:20 makes "no license stated at all" the documented escalate-to-human case, so identifier-absent + override is the intended path, and the defect is the None rendering), and do not add a human_override.waives list of issue identifiers (see rejected).

docs.title: 3. license.md instructs prose in the two fields the gate matches against fixed vocabularies
docs.text:
Confidence: verified. Cost: small (doc + optional schema split).

license.md:127 says redistribution — "allowed, or a description of the restriction". license.md:133-134 says "Quote the restriction in your own words in upstream_license if it has no SPDX name". gates.py:427-432 errors on any redistribution not in ('allowed','yes','permitted'); gates.py:477-483 runs is_permissive() — a set membership test against 15 SPDX-ish tokens — on upstream_license.

So the documented way to fill these fields guarantees a false escalation. redistribution: 'allowed with attribution' — the natural CC-BY phrasing — ERRORs. upstream_license: 'Public domain; PubChem places no restrictions on use or redistribution.' ERRORs, directly contradicting SKILL.md:300-304's claim that "a named upstream whose own license is permissive passes without ceremony".

Change. Split each field: redistribution becomes an enum (allowed | restricted | unknown) with free-text redistribution_note; upstream_license becomes upstream_license_id (SPDX or none) plus free-text upstream_license_note, with is_permissive applied only to the id. Update license.md's "What to report" block and both SKILL.md examples. Fix SKILL.md:318-319 to say what is true after item 2 lands.

Risk. A schema change to a persisted manifest section; old manifests carry the old keys. Accept both for one release, or migrate on load.

docs.title: 4. crwl -o markdown-fit is a content-pruning mode, and there is no implausible-output check
docs.text:
Confidence: verified. Cost: tiny (two string edits + one paragraph).

SKILL.md:150 makes crwl '<url>' -o markdown-fit the reader for every page, and troubleshooting.md:146 repeats it. markdown-fit is crawl4ai's pruning mode. Measured on the elanos_bp source article: -o markdown = 234,604 bytes, -o markdown-fit = 160,678 bytes (31.5% pruned); grep -c 'Full size table' = 10 vs 0. Those anchors are the only route to https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11030-025-11196-5/tables/2, which reads BP | − 88.60 | 548.00 | 188.98 ± 85.07 — degrees Celsius, i.e. the evidence that disproves the shipped script's "in Kelvin". SKILL.md:475 tells the stage-6 subagent to check "that the target values are in the range the paper reports"; the mandated reader mode deletes the route to that range. grep -rn -i table across SKILL.md and all five references returns no mention of publisher table pages at all.

Separately, crwl 'https://db.chempharos.eu/datasets/Datasets.zul' -o markdown returns 1 byte, exit 0, while curl -sL -A 'Mozilla/5.0' on the same URL returns 11,194 bytes containing the upstream provenance the license gate requires. The skill's fallback ladder (SKILL.md:148-163) is keyed on failure; a 1-byte exit-0 read is not a failure.

Change. (a) Change both occurrences to -o markdown. Add one sentence: markdown-fit prunes low-density blocks by design — it drops boilerplate but also drops tables, figure captions and short link-only sections. Never for the first read of an article. (b) Add an implausible-output rule to the tools section: after every page read, check the byte count and check the output contains a token you expect from that page class (an article: availability or supporting; a repository record: a filename or download). Under ~2 KB, or missing the token, is a failed read — go to the next reader. Add curl -A 'Mozilla/5.0' to the ladder as the reader that wins on Ajax/ZK apps where content sits in hidden divs. (c) Add a "publisher tables and figures live at their own URLs" note to data-sources.md with the Springer /article/<doi>/tables/<n> form.

This is the whole of known-outstanding item 1, and it is the cheapest item on this list.

docs.title: 5. No gate reads the run's own record — a crashed run passes all six
docs.text:
Confidence: verified. Cost: small-medium (~40 lines + test fixture update).

pycomex writes experiment_meta.json (name, status, has_error, start_time, and every parameter's actual value including __TESTING__) and experiment_code.py (a byte copy of the executing module — sha256 of the real run's copy equals the on-disk script) into every results directory. No gate opens either. gate_execute instead decides whether testing mode was on by regexing the current source text (gates.py:635), which describes the file now, not the run.

Reproduced consequences:

  • A results directory with status='failed' / has_error=True and everything else intact passes gate_script, gate_execute and gate_verification with zero issues. The base template writes .mpack, .mpack.gz and metadata.yml before the final after_save hook — the hook the extraction agent routinely writes itself — so a run that crashes in the agent's own code ships.
  • A script edited an hour after the run, whose experiment_code.py literally reads OLD VERSION OF THE SCRIPT, passes all three gates.
  • smoke_results_dir and results_dir are the identical string in the real manifest (…/create_graph_datasets__enalos_bp/debug), because SKILL.md:419 and SKILL.md:437 prescribe the same path — and __DEBUG__ shutil.rmtrees that folder at the start of the next run, so by the time gate_script runs, the smoke output physically does not exist. gate_script on the real manifest returns ok=True with zero issues while inspecting a 5432-compound __TESTING__=False full run and reporting it as the smoke run.
  • Nothing ties a results directory to the script. Pointing smoke_results_dir at any other single-target dataset's debug folder passes.

Change, in this order of value per line:

  1. _check_run_provenance(results_dir, script_path) used by gate_execute and gate_verification: ERROR when has_error is true or status != 'done'; ERROR when meta['name'] != Path(script_path).stem. Three checks, no false-positive surface, closes the crashed-run and wrong-directory holes outright. Do this even if you do nothing else in this item.
  2. Missing/unparseable experiment_meta.json → WARNING, not ERROR. Fatal-with-no-override is a dead end for archived or relocated folders, and gates sys.exit(1) with no --force.
  3. In gate_execute, replace the __TESTING__ source regex with meta['parameters']['__TESTING__']['value']. The regex has a live false positive today: __TESTING__ = False # (was True during the smoke run) hard-blocks the run.
  4. Run the structural block (gates.py:542-573) against <results_dir>/experiment_code.py in gate_execute, extracted as check_script_structure(source) -> list[VerificationIssue]. Today those five checks run exactly once, on a file the workflow guarantees will be edited before the run (SKILL.md:407 mandates __TESTING__ = True, SKILL.md:428 mandates False). Of the five, .dataset_work is the one a stage-5 debugging edit plausibly introduces.
  5. In gate_verification only, compare experiment_code.py against the working script and warn (not error) when they differ, printing both short hashes. Skip when experiment_config.yml is present — save_code writes a stub, not a copy, for config-based experiments.
  6. Two SKILL.md lines: run the smoke as python chem_mat_data/scripts/create_graph_datasets__<name>.py --__TESTING__ True --__DEBUG__ False and record the unique timestamped folder pycomex prints. The script file is then never edited between smoke and full run, both runs' evidence survives, and smoke_results_dir != results_dir by construction. (This step is likely, not verified: it depends on ExperimentArgumentParser.parse eval'ing CLI values, which one investigator confirmed but I did not re-run.)

Risk. write_results (tests/test_agent_pipeline.py:565) emits neither file, so 15 tests in TestScriptGate/TestExecuteGate break until the fixture emits an experiment_code.py matching the script it wrote and a meta whose name equals the script stem. That is a fixture-coupling refactor, and test_testing_flag_left_on_is_an_error changes meaning. Do not hash the script against smoke_results_dir/experiment_code.py in gate_script — the mandated __TESTING__ flip makes that mismatch by design, and gates have no override. Do not make the hash an ERROR anywhere: two of run 2's four verification fixes were comment-only, and a full run "can take hours".

This closes known-outstanding item 2. Note that step 1 and step 6 are independent; step 6 is what actually makes the smoke check non-vacuous, and it costs two documentation lines.

docs.title: 6. source_url is still settable in code, and fixing that re-arms a warning that will now fire on every run
docs.text:
Confidence: verified. Cost: small.

e39f0c4 documented source_url as "set once by init" in SKILL.md:68-74. agent set still accepts it (manage.py:1978), and manage.py:481-485's own help text still lists it first among the freely settable scalars. The prose and the tool disagree, which is exactly how the original defect happened: the real manifest records source_url: https://zenodo.org/records/14392754/files/BP.csv?download=1.

The compound problem: with the download URL in source_url, the host-divergence warning (gates.py:486-495) compares zenodo.org against zenodo.org and stays silent — I confirmed it did not fire in run 2. Restore the correct Springer URL and it fires immediately. So e39f0c4's doc fix converts known-outstanding item 4 from a hypothetical into a certainty: every ordinary paper-on-publisher / data-on-repository run will now warn.

The root cause is that the manifest has no field for the direct download URL, so an agent that has just spent stage 1 establishing it has literally nowhere to record it.

Change. Remove source_url from the scalars dict and reject it with an error naming init --url. Add record_url (the repository landing page) and data_url (the direct download) as settable scalars. Have gate_license compare the evidence host against record_url when present and source_url otherwise — which is the correct comparison anyway, since the question the warning exists for is "is the file we downloaded covered by the license we read", not "did the paper and the data live on the same host". Fix manage.py:483.

Risk. Removing a settable key breaks any in-flight run that expects it; the error message must name the replacement.

docs.title: 7. The final gate never compares target_descriptions or dataset_name
docs.text:
Confidence: verified. Cost: small.

gate_verification compares ('verbose','description') at gates.py:741 and ('tags','sources') at gates.py:754. Nothing else. Probed on the real manifest: replacing the draft's target_descriptions with 'BP - boiling point in KELVIN, log-transformed', dataset_type with 'classification' and dataset_name with 'something_else' → ok=True, zero issues. target_descriptions is the only per-target place units live, and dataset_name is the identifier a downstream user types into load_smiles_dataset. gates.py:709-710's docstring claims the gate "confirms that what ended up in metadata.yml actually matches what the metadata stage approved". (SKILL.md:383-385 already states the truth correctly, so the docstring is the only place that overclaims.)

Change. Compare target_descriptions index-by-index after normalize_target_description_keys at WARNING on divergence (matching how verbose/description are already treated) and ERROR when an index approved in the draft is missing or empty. ERROR when draft['dataset_type'] is not in written['target_type'] — categorical, so a mismatch is unambiguous, and across all 45 catalog entries target_type is uniformly ['regression'] or ['classification']. ERROR when the .mpack stem does not equal draft['dataset_name']. Fix the docstring. Document --strict at stage 6, which makes every warning blocking at the final gate for zero code change.

Be honest about what this buys. It catches transcription drift between the approved draft and the METADATA literal. It would not have caught the "in Kelvin" defect: that script has no manifest and never went through the skill, and an agent confidently wrong about units writes the same wrong string into both sides. See item 9 for the check that would.

Do not promote the missing-' - '-separator warning to ERROR, and do not add a description[i].split(' - ')[0] == TARGET_COLUMNS[i] check (both in rejected).

docs.title: 8. The .mpack and the .csv of the same run are a full permutation of each other
docs.text:
Confidence: verified. Cost: medium.

Measured on the real run: 5432 graphs, 5432 CSV rows, 5432/5432 positional mismatches, identical sorted multisets. mpack[:3] = ['CC(C)CCC(CC)CC', 'CC(CC)(CC)C(O)=O', 'C[C@@H](N)C(C)(C)C'] against csv[:3] = ['C=O', 'OC(=O)c1cc(Cl)ccc1Cl', 'CN(C)CN(C)C']. Content is intact; only row order diverges. Anyone joining the two artifacts by row index silently mismatches every compound.

Cause: create_graph_datasets.py:357 feeds workers with indices.pop() (from the tail) and appends graphs in completion order, while save_csv (lines 256-284) iterates the dataset in insertion order. Second, independent bug: save_csv is applied at lines 324-326, before the __TESTING__ truncation at 333-337, so every smoke run writes a full-length CSV next to a 50-graph mpack.

This is in the shared base template, so it affects every dataset in the repository, not just skill-produced ones. verify_results (verification.py:186-190) checks only that both files exist.

Change. Carry the source index through the worker and sort graphs back into dataset order before saving; move the save_csv call after the __TESTING__ truncation; set allow_unicode=True on yaml.dump at create_graph_datasets.py:458 (this is where the \xB0C escape in the known-outstanding list comes from — it is cosmetic, since yaml.safe_load round-trips it correctly, but the file is meant to be human-readable). Add a cross-artifact check to verify_results: CSV row count must equal compounds, and the first N mpack SMILES must equal the corresponding CSV rows.

Risk. Changing row order changes the bytes of every dataset the next time it is regenerated; if any downstream consumer has pinned an index-based split, it breaks. Worth checking before shipping. The verify_results cross-check will fail on every existing results directory until the template fix lands — sequence them.

docs.title: 9. Units have no check at all; record the source-stated range and check it
docs.text:
Confidence: likely (the streaming implementation was measured; the manifest field is new design). Cost: medium.

Units are the highest-consequence claim the pipeline makes and the only one with no verification anywhere. Nothing in the manifest records what the paper says the values should look like, so stage 6's instruction to check "that the target values are in the range the paper reports" (SKILL.md:475) has no reference point recorded anywhere and no mechanical backstop.

Change. Add target_ranges to metadata_draft: per target index, the min/max/mean the source states, plus the URL it was read from (null with an explicit reason when the source states none). gate_metadata requires the key present for regression datasets. In gate_execute, stream the labels out of the .mpack with msgpack.Unpacker(f, ext_hook=…) + read_array_header() — one graph at a time, accumulating min/max/mean/n_unique per target index — and ERROR when the observed range falls outside the declared range beyond tolerance, WARN when it is a suspiciously narrow subset. Print the per-target summary statistics unconditionally, so the stage-6 subagent has numbers to hold against the paper instead of having to compute them itself.

Measured: streaming is 0.08 s / 3 MB RSS on the real 29 MB mpack, versus 0.09 s / 69 MB for load_graphs, and it scales to the 19.4 GB mpacks in this repo that load_graphs cannot touch. Never call load_graphs in a gate.

This is the only proposal on the list that could have caught "in Kelvin" (declared −88.6 to 548.0 against a Kelvin claim), and it is the only one that catches a wrong TARGET_COLUMNS (D001's range is 0..1). It depends on item 4(c) to make publisher table pages reachable.

Risk. A new required field in metadata_draft blocks existing in-flight runs. Papers that state no ranges need the explicit-null-with-reason path or the requirement becomes an invitation to fabricate numbers, which is worse than no check.

docs.title: 10. gate_prepare accepts anything non-empty that does not start with <html
docs.text:
Confidence: verified. Cost: small in the reduced form (~30 lines).

gates.py:211-218 checks st_size > 0 and an HTML byte prefix, and nothing else. All of the following pass with ok=True: BP.csv containing Not Found; a Zenodo JSON record dump saved as BP.csv; smiles,BP\n and nothing else; <?xml version="1.0"?><error>access denied</error>. gates.py:231 requires only that the substring http appears somewhere in the recipe, so see the paper at http://doi.org/10.1000/xyz passes while recording nothing the script stage can build a download from. Conversely, a legitimate two-row license_compounds.csv is rejected — NON_DATA_NAMES (gates.py:70) is matched as a bare substring of the filename.

Severity is capped: the script must be self-contained, so a garbage scratch download surfaces at the smoke run (no .mpack dataset file found, smoke run produced 0 compounds). The cost is two wasted stages, not a shipped-wrong dataset. The one genuinely silent case is a truncated-but-parseable download: the agent types input_rows from the partial copy, the script downloads the full file, and gate_execute only warns when compounds > input_rows — so an unnoticed truncation converts the execute gate's one quantitative safeguard into a no-op.

Change. (a) Directory-level, not per-file: ERROR unless at least one file in the downloads dir parses as a table with ≥1 data row (sep=None, engine='python'; no ≥2-columns requirement — a single-column SMILES list is legitimate). This catches every demonstrated case while leaving ancillary JSON and prose files alone. (b) Match NON_DATA_NAMES against the filename stem with word boundaries, and list the excluded files in the "no data files" error so it is diagnosable. (c) Promote compounds > input_rows from WARNING to ERROR (gates.py:653-658), with the same max_drop_rate-style escape hatch the drop check has. This is the actual fix for the silent case. (d) Recipe check: require at least one URL whose host is not doi.org/dx.doi.org. (e) Reword the "no README captured — units will have to be inferred" warning to "no schema documentation captured", and fire it only when neither a README nor a schema section in the recipe is present. In the real run the agent's own download_recipe.md documented the 798 columns, the units and the value range better than any README would, and the gate warned anyway. (Known-outstanding item 5.)

Do not add a per-suffix parse dispatch, a JSON "repository record" heuristic, or a rule matching URL final segments against downloaded filenames — all three block legitimate runs (see rejected).

docs.title: 11. A blocked run cannot record why
docs.text:
Confidence: verified mechanism, projected harm. Cost: small.

SKILL.md:78-113 teaches the agent to compose a good escalation — what is blocking, what was tried with specific URLs and tools, what is needed — and then SKILL.md:105 tells it to persist that by running cmmanage agent gate <stage> <slug>, which records the gate's mechanical first error instead. On a paywalled paper the manifest ends up saying no data files in the downloads directory (only README/recipe files were found). agent set rejects blocker and notes outright (manage.py:1985-1996), so the information has nowhere to go.

The sharper defect, which matters more than the missing prose: BLOCKED is not a human-escalation marker. --record defaults on, so any failed gate marks BLOCKED, including ones the agent fixes thirty seconds later. A resuming reader cannot distinguish "needs a human with an ACS subscription" from "the agent hadn't written the draft yet".

Change. With item 1(b) done (all errors recorded, not just the first), add one command: cmmanage agent block <stage> <slug> --why <one line> --tried <text> --need <text>, which sets needs_human: true on the stage state so agent status can render ✗ blocked — needs a human: <why> versus ✗ blocked — gate failure, resumable. Run it after the gate, and say so at SKILL.md:102-105: the gate records the symptom, agent block records the diagnosis.

Also fix Manifest.mark (manifest.py:343) to preserve blocker and notes unless new ones are passed, instead of constructing a fresh StageState. Today agent block followed by agent gate — the ordering the original proposal prescribed — silently erases everything the block command wrote. A status change is not a reason to forget why.

Risk. needs_human on StageState touches to_dict/from_dict; old manifests must load with it absent (manifest.py:109-116 already tolerates missing keys). Do not add agent note — no demonstrated demand.

docs.title: 12. Manifest durability, and no way to find a run again
docs.text:
Confidence: verified. Cost: small.

Three separate small things in the state layer, cheap enough to do in one session:

  • manifest.py:297-298 rewrites the file in place with a plain truncating open, no temp file, no backup — on every agent set and every agent gate. load() then does the worst possible thing with damage: StageState.from_dict returns a pending state for any non-dict (manifest.py:109-110) and absent stages are filled in as pending (manifest.py:235-238), so a manifest truncated to slug: g\nsource_url: https://x loads without error reporting that nothing has been done. A resuming agent re-downloads, re-licenses and re-scripts a completed run, losing the human's override. Fix: temp + os.replace, a .bak copy, and raise on a missing slug/created_at/stages mapping rather than defaulting to pending.
  • The agent group registers only venv, tools, verify, init, status, gate, set (manage.py:825-832). There is no way to enumerate .dataset_work/, so a human returning to a blocked run must already know its slug. Add agent list: slug, dataset name, next stage, status, blocker first line, age, sorted blocked-first.
  • init --force (manage.py:1782-1789) constructs a fresh manifest over the old one, deleting a recorded license.human_override — a human's verbatim words, often the product of an email exchange — while leaving the downloads that made the run cheap to resume. Rename the existing file to manifest.<created_at>.yml instead, and refuse outright when human_override is present unless a separate explicit flag is given, quoting the recorded decision in the error.

Also worth noting and not fixing here: agent set writes the entire manifest payload with zero staleness invalidation (manage.py:1956-2020 never calls mark()). Replacing metadata_draft, results_dir and script_path on a fully-passed run leaves all six stages passed. The staleness model guards gate, but set is where state actually changes. This is the mechanism by which an ERROR added anywhere is trivially cleared by rewriting the draft to match whatever the script says — worth knowing before relying on any new ERROR.

docs.title: 13. Two smaller instruction defects
docs.text:
Confidence: verified. Cost: tiny.

  • SKILL.md:52 and SKILL.md:485 say "re-run" a stale stage. For execute — whose own text warns "This can take hours" — that reads as an instruction to reprocess the dataset.
