Gates execute nothing; they read files. Measured on the real completed run: script 2.5 ms, execute 2.0 ms, verification 3.6 ms, all ok=True. And license.md:181 routes every CC-BY dataset with an attribution requirement — the most common passing license — straight into that cascade by design. Replace with: "Re-run its gate first — the results on disk are untouched and it normally re-passes in well under a second. Only redo the stage's work if the gate then fails."
  • SKILL.md:385-387 documents a failure mode that does not exist. It says putting description only in METADATA and not in DESCRIPTION "is the way to fail that gate at the very last stage". create_graph_datasets.py:453 does metadata.update(e.METADATA), so METADATA['description'] lands in metadata.yml and matches the draft — it passes. The instruction trains the reader to guard against the wrong thing. Replace with the true statement: the template merges METADATA over the derived fields, so whichever of DESCRIPTION / METADATA['description'] you set must match the approved draft verbatim.
  • examples/xyz_3d.py contradicts the stage-4 non-negotiable it illustrates. SKILL.md:371-373 says load_dataset must download from the original URL and must not read .dataset_work/. The example sets SOURCE_PATH = ~/Downloads/qm9.xyz_bundle, contains no download code at all (grep 'requests|urlretrieve|FileDownloadSource' → nothing), and passes gate_script's self-containment check only because re.search(r'https?://', source) (gates.py:569) is satisfied by the two DOIs sitting in METADATA['sources']. Either give the example real download logic or label it as the one archetype where the data is fetched by the intermediate base.

Also worth two lines in SKILL.md while editing: the skill has zero coverage of a paper that publishes several datasets (grep -rn -i 'multiple dataset|several dataset|each dataset' across all nine skill files returns nothing), while the elanos_bp source paper publishes nine across nine repository records, and the manifest is single-valued throughout. State the rule: one slug per shippable dataset; enumerate them first and say so to the user. And specify input_rows properly — SKILL.md:206's trailing comment "rows in the raw source, for the drop check" is its entire specification, for the number that drives the pipeline's only defence against silent data loss.

docs.title: 14. Resolve citations against the DOI registry
docs.text:
Confidence: verified that the mechanism works; the gate integration is design. Cost: medium.

The pipeline's output is a citable scientific artifact whose provenance is entirely agent-authored prose, and no gate reads any of it. In run 2 the agent invented a paper title with the wrong first author in its own download recipe, and the license subagent caught it outside its brief — by luck. gate_metadata requires sources to be a non-empty list (gates.py:301-303) and nothing more, so a hallucinated DOI ships.

One endpoint covers both registries: curl -sL -H 'Accept: application/vnd.citationstyles.csl+json' https://doi.org/<doi> returns CSL-JSON via Crossref for the Springer DOI (title, first author Koutroumpa, Nikoletta-Maria), via DataCite for the Zenodo DOI, and HTML for a fabricated one. ~1 s per DOI.

Change. cmmanage agent cite <slug> <doi> fetches and stores the registry record verbatim under citations[<doi>]. gate_metadata then requires every DOI-shaped entry in sources to have a resolved record; gate_license requires evidence_url's DOI, when it has one, to be among them; the skill instructs the agent to compose citation prose from the stored records rather than from memory. Add --offline degrading to a warning.

Cheaper alternative if that is too much machinery: widen the stage-3 subagent's brief from "license" to "provenance and license" and make citation verification an explicit deliverable. That converts run 2's luckiest catch into a process, for the cost of one paragraph — and given the structural conclusion at the top of this document, it may be the better trade.

docs.title: Considered and rejected
docs.text:
Reconcile the produced dataset against the raw source instead of counting rows. Provably cannot detect what it exists to detect: it reads SMILES_COLUMN/TARGET_COLUMNS out of the run's own experiment_meta.json and then reads those same columns from raw_data.csv, so the sets match by construction. Demonstrated by building three genuine datasets from the real raw_data.csv (correct columns; TARGET_COLUMNS=['D001']; SMILES_COLUMN='Canonical SMILES') — absent-fraction 0.00% for all three. It also hard-fails every classification dataset built with the repo's one-hot pattern (15 of 71 scripts) and every log/unit-transformed target (6 scripts), raw_data.csv is present in 0 of 51 real results dirs, and load_graphs would need ~65 GB peak on the largest mpack. Replaced by item 9, which sources the expectation from the paper rather than from the run.

Split the manifest into source-scoped and dataset-scoped state with a DEPENDS_ON graph. The motivating scenario is structurally unreachable — run_gate refuses to gate script while license has not passed, so the "human approves an override days later and invalidates the multi-hour run" event cannot happen. When re-gating is reachable it costs 2-4 ms, not hours (measured). And the proposed dependency map omits prepare → license, although gate_license reads manifest.source_url — so a prepare re-run landing on a different record would leave a license established against the old record marked passed, reintroducing the run-1 failure class. Positional invalidation over-invalidates cheaply and never under-invalidates a safety-relevant edge; keep it. Fix the wording instead (item 13).

Cache the license finding across a paper's sibling datasets. license.md:6-9 runs the license stage as a fresh subagent deliberately: "an agent with no stake in the outcome reads the terms as they are." Both runs' best catches came from that independence. Nine independent investigations are nine replications of the only safety check, not nine chances to disagree; the disagreement is the signal. Also the license is not source-scoped in the motivating example — the paper's nine datasets live in nine separate Zenodo records with per-record license fields. If the rediscovery cost matters, agent init <slug> --from <sibling> handing the sibling's conclusion to the fresh subagent as prior art it must agree or disagree with gets the saving without losing the independence.

Pin script_sha256 in the manifest. By the proposer's own reasoning the digest always differs at the execute gate (the mandated __TESTING__ flip), so the conditional carries no information. It also requires gates to mutate the manifest, which today happens exclusively in agent_gate_command. experiment_code.py is already a byte-exact record written by the runner rather than by the agent being policed — use it (item 5).

Require an identifier before an override can be approved, and a human_override.waives list of issue identifiers. license.md:124 says to omit identifier entirely rather than guess, and license.md:20 makes "no license stated at all" the documented escalate-to-human case — so identifier-absent + override is the intended path, and the defect is the None rendering. VerificationIssue is level + free-text message with 69 report.add() sites; adding a code taxonomy makes persisted manifest schema that can never be reworded, and the extraction agent would author both the license blob and the waives list, so it buys no oversight.

Promote the missing-' - '-separator warning to ERROR. 43 of 484 shipped descriptions lack the separator, whole datasets at a time (tmqmg 20/20, tmqm 8/8, kulik_spin 7/7). It is style, and test_description_without_separator_is_a_warning asserts the current behaviour by name. --strict already covers anyone who wants it blocking.

Have gate_execute assert description[i].split(' - ')[0] == TARGET_COLUMNS[i]. Breaks six shipped scripts, including half_life — the script the skill itself produced in validation run 1 — and both binary-classification scripts, whose one-hot pattern produces more descriptions than TARGET_COLUMNS entries. It also contradicts metadata.md:82, which teaches a semantic label as the head for classification targets.

Derive input_rows from the downloaded scratch file. The denominator would come from a copy that may itself be truncated, arriving labelled "derived, not typed" and trusted accordingly. Promote compounds > input_rows to ERROR instead (item 10c) — that compares the typed denominator against the script's own acquisition of the source.

Demote the preprint/published host-divergence warning. It reverses part of e39f0c4, and a "both hosts are publication venues" test needs a hardcoded venue allowlist that would suppress the paper-on-Springer / SI-elsewhere case. Compare against record_url instead (item 6) — that is the comparison the warning should have been making from the start.

Per-format parse dispatch in gate_prepare, a JSON "repository record" heuristic, and matching URL final segments against downloaded filenames. The JSON rule would have blocked the only end-to-end run the skill has ever passed — that run's downloads directory legitimately contains zenodo_record_14392754.json as provenance. The URL rule is wrong by construction for figshare (ndownloader/files/<id>), OSF and Dryad, three of the eight hosts documented in data-sources.md. pd.read_csv(nrows=5) with a ≥2-column requirement hard-errors on semicolon-separated CSV, single-column SMILES lists and prose .txt documentation. A false ERROR here is more expensive than a false pass, because the pass is caught at the smoke run while the ERROR stops a correct run dead.

agent note (an append-only timestamped log in the manifest). No demonstrated demand from either validation run. With all gate errors and warnings persisted (item 1), nothing remains for it to carry.

docs.title: Dataset licence review — the 41 that need a decision
docs.text:
Status: open. Awaiting maintainer decisions. Generated 2026-08-19 from a 92-agent research pass over 46 unlabelled datasets.

Each dataset was researched by its own agent (licence on the data, not the article; upstream provenance named explicitly) and then assessed against the policy in .claude/skills/dataset-extraction/references/license.md. Three were clear enough to apply automatically. Two more were already decided and are recorded below. The remaining 41 need a person, but they are not 41 separate questions - they collapse into ten families, and four of those families account for 17 datasets.

Nothing in this file has been applied. No script was edited for any dataset listed here.

docs.text:
Dataset Licence How hopv15_exp CC-BY-4.0 Applied automatically - Figshare record states it pfas_classify CC0-1.0 Applied automatically - Figshare record states it reactaivate MIT Applied automatically - repo LICENSE, the only record the paper names pka_water CC0-1.0 Applied from your existing 2026-08-13 approval pka_acidic CC0-1.0 Applied from your existing 2026-08-13 approval

docs.title: ZINC — 5 datasets
docs.text:
Five datasets whose structures trace to ZINC. One decision about ZINC's terms settles all five.

Dataset Own licence Conf. Redistribution Upstream qm40_smiles CC-BY-4.0 high allowed ZINC qm40_xyz CC-BY-4.0 high allowed ZINC synth_binary_global none-found low restricted ZINC (ZINC15/ZINC12, Shoichet Lab, UCSF — docking.org), via the ZINC-250k subset… synth_binary_local LicenseRef-ZINC-Terms-of-Use medium restricted ZINC (docking.org, Irwin & Shoichet labs / UC Regents) — the 250k random drug-li… zinc250k Apache-2.0 medium restricted ZINC

qm40_smiles — Researcher found CC-BY-4.0 stated directly on the Figshare data record (article 25993060, high confidence) for the QM40 SMILES/property compilation itself — that part is clean. But QM40's underlying molecules are a screened subset of ZINC (162,954 of ZINC20's ~1B, ~0.016%) and the script keeps ZINC ids as graph_id, so ZINC's own terms of use are also in play. Those terms are custom, not SPDX-permissive: sharing 'results of a screen' is allowed, but redistributing 'major portions' of ZINC requires John Irwin's written permission (chemistry4biology@gmail.com). The researcher's own reasoning is that 0.016% clearly isn't a 'major portion' so redistribution is fine, but that's an interpretive judgment call on an undefined term, not a stated grant — exactly the kind of upstream-database question the policy reserves for a human. Decide: (a) accept the researcher's 'not a major portion' reading · evidence: https://api.figshare.com/v2/articles/25993060

qm40_xyz — Do not apply. The data itself (QM40 Figshare record 10.6084/m9.figshare.25993060.v1) is CC-BY-4.0 with high confidence — verified via the Figshare API against the exact file the script downloads (MD5-matched), corroborated by the paper's Code availability section. That part alone would pass. But the molecular identities (ZINC ids/SMILES retained as graph_id) come from ZINC, whose docking.org terms of use are custom/bespoke — not CC0/CC-BY/MIT/BSD/Apache/ODC-BY — and explicitly state: "you may not redistribute major portions of ZINC without the express written permission of John Irwin." The researcher argues this doesn't apply because QM40's ~163k molecules are a small fraction (~0.02-0.07%) of ZINC's ~700M and fall under ZINC's own carve-out for sharing "the results of a ZINC search or a screen," but that is an interpretive judgment call about a non-permissive upstream licence, exactly w · evidence: https://figshare.com/articles/dataset/QM40_A_More_Realistic_QM_Dataset_for_Machine_Learning_in_Molecular_Science/25993060

synth_binary_global — Do not apply a license to synth_binary_global; it needs a human decision. The 249,455 SMILES in this dataset are the ZINC-250k subset (Gomez-Bombarelli et al. 2018, itself drawn from ZINC/docking.org, Shoichet Lab UCSF) — confirmed by matching compound count against the sibling zinc250k dataset already in this repo. ZINC's own terms of use (https://wiki.docking.org/index.php/ZINC) say it is "freely available to everyone to use" but that "significant portions... may not be re-distributed without express written permission of John Irwin" — free-to-use, not free-to-redistribute, with no SPDX equivalent. The three plausible download mirrors give conflicting/non-authoritative signals: Kaggle's copy self-declares ODbL-1.0 (ShareAlike copyleft — would itself escalate, and an uploader who isn't the rights holder can't grant ZINC's rights anyway); the chemical_vae GitHub repo wraps the CSV in a r · evidence: https://wiki.docking.org/index.php/ZINC

synth_binary_local — Do not apply a licence to synth_binary_local — escalate to a human. The dataset's 249,455 molecules are byte-identical to ZINC's public "250k_rndm_zinc_drugs_clean_3.csv" (the ChemicalVAE 250k subset); the labels are ChemMatData's own SMARTS-derived synthetic classification, so the only third-party content redistributed is the ZINC SMILES themselves. ZINC's live terms of use (wiki.docking.org/index.php/Terms_And_Conditions, current revision dated 2025-03-21) permit sharing "the results of a ZINC search or a screen of molecules from ZINC" but forbid redistributing "major portions of ZINC without the express written permission of John Irwin" — a threshold ZINC never defines. The chemical_vae GitHub repo that hosts the file carries a blanket Apache-2.0 LICENSE.txt, but that grant comes from the ChemicalVAE authors (A. Dorsk / Aspuru-Guzik group), who hold no rights in the ZINC compound coll · evidence: https://wiki.docking.org/index.php/Terms_And_Conditions

zinc250k — Do not apply a license to zinc250k (script: chem_mat_data/scripts/create_graph_datasets__zinc250k.py) — the file was not edited. docs.title: How to work through this
docs.text:
The families are ordered roughly easiest-first. A decision on one family applies to every dataset in it, so the four upstream families at the top (ZINC, GDB, EPI Suite, PubChem) settle 17 datasets between them.

For each family the question is the same one you answered for ChEMBL: does the upstream's licence permit redistribution, and if it carries an obligation, is the project willing to pass that obligation on? The machinery to record the answer already exists - the license field, ADR 009, and the Settled section of rejected_datasets.md.

A caution about the research. Confidence is self-reported by the agent that did the work. Where it says low, treat the finding as a starting point rather than a conclusion: in several cases the agent could not reach the source at all, and "no licence found" then means "not found by this agent" rather than "none exists". The high-confidence rows quote licence text they actually read.

docs.title: Redistributing Ilm-NMR-P31: upstream licensing and the "link, don't host" proposal
docs.text: This is not legal advice, and I am not a lawyer. It is a research memo describing how the relevant law is generally understood, written so that the maintainer can put sharp questions to KIT's legal office instead of vague ones. Every legal source cited below was fetched and read; where I could not verify something I say so inline, marked [UNVERIFIED]. Do not act on this without the legal office signing off on the two or three points flagged as decisive.

docs.title: Q1 — "The authors already published it, so it's more or less public. Can we take it?"
docs.text:
No, that reasoning is wrong — but the conclusion is closer to "yes, mostly" than you'd expect, for entirely different reasons.

Publishing something under CC-BY-4.0 cannot grant rights the publisher never held. The licence says so itself: the grant is limited to rights "that the Licensor has authority to license" (CC BY 4.0 §1(7)), and §5(a) expressly disclaims any warranty of title or non-infringement. So the CC-BY tag on the Zenodo record is not a shield. That is the nemo dat point and it is correct.

But "is it protected at all?" is the question that actually decides this, and the answer splits the dataset cleanly in two:

Source block 3D structures EU database right Status HBP — Tebby, CRC Press, 1991 6,608 Term expired 31 Dec 2012 (§137g(2) UrhG); maker is US, likely outside Art. 11 Very likely clean Lan1/2/3 — Landolt-Börnstein III/40H, Springer, 2013/14 5,114 Term runs to ~2029; German maker; investment is in obtaining, not creating This is the exposure NMRexp (journal-scraped) 0 — n/a

The individual chemical-shift values are not protected as such anywhere — not in Germany, not in the US. What is potentially protected is the compilation. And the compilation right on the larger of the two blocks (56% of your 3D structures) ran out thirteen years ago.

So the honest position is: the Landolt-Börnstein-derived 5,114 structures are the problem, and they are separable. Your source column already distinguishes them. See the middle path below.

docs.title: Q2 — "What if we fetch from Zenodo instead of hosting it ourselves?"
docs.text:
Legally it does not help you, and it is the wrong counterparty. Engineering-wise it is a structural change, not a small one, and it destroys the main thing the project is for.

Not hosting avoids "extraction". It does not avoid "re-utilisation", which is defined as "any form of making available to the public ... by ... on-line or other forms of transmission" (Art. 7(2)(b), Directive 96/9/EC). The CJEU in Innoweb held that an operator who merely publishes a retrieval mechanism re-utilises the database — the mechanism "comes close to the manufacture of a parasitical competing product ... albeit without copying the information stored in the database concerned" (C‑202/12, para 48). CV-Online puts it even more bluntly: hyperlinks are "merely external manifestations, of secondary importance, of that extraction and that re-utilisation" (C‑762/19, para 37).

And the deeper problem: the party you'd be linking to is not the party with the complaint. The Ilm-NMR authors already consented — their CC-BY grant over their own layer is valid. Springer never consented to anything and is not on the other end of that link. Routing through Zenodo changes nothing about Springer's position.

On the engineering side: connectors.py already contains a ZenodoSource, but it is imported only by the build-time create_graph_datasets__*.py scripts. Nothing in the load path touches it. Wiring it into main.py:ensure_dataset() means a new source abstraction, a version-aware cache (the current one is keyed on {name}.{typ} with no version and no checksum), a pinned client-side processing pipeline, a 155 MB download per user instead of a gzipped .mpack, and the loss of offline use. Details below.

docs.title: 1. The analysis: what is actually protected
1.1 The individual shift values — not protected, clearly
docs.text:
Three independent confirmations, and this one is not close:

  • Recital 45, Directive 96/9/EC: "the right to prevent unauthorized extraction and/or re-utilization does not in any way constitute an extension of copyright protection to mere facts or data."
  • Recital 46: the right "should not give rise to the creation of a new right in the works, data or materials themselves."
  • Art. 3(2): "The copyright protection of databases ... shall not extend to their contents."

German law is the same: §2(2) UrhG protects only a persönliche geistige Schöpfung, which a measured ppm value is not. In the US, Feist reaches the identical result by a different route: "No one may claim originality as to facts ... The distinction is one between creation and discovery: The first person to find and report a particular fact has not created the fact" (499 U.S. 340).

So nobody can stop you from using a ³¹P shift value. The fight, if there is one, is over taking the collection.

docs.title: 1.2 Do the books count as "databases" at all? — Yes
docs.text:
This was the right question to ask, and the answer is yes, printed reference works qualify. Art. 1(2) defines a database as a collection "individually accessible by electronic or other means" — the "or other means" is doing exactly this work. The CJEU confirmed the breadth in Fixtures Marketing v OPAP: the term "refers to any collection of works, data or other materials, separable from one another without the value of their contents being affected, including a method or system of some sort for the retrieval of each of its constituent materials" (C‑444/02, summary point 1).

A ³¹P NMR reference table indexed by compound is squarely inside that. Germany transposes it identically in §87a(1) UrhG ("einzeln mit Hilfe elektronischer Mittel oder auf andere Weise zugänglich").

docs.title: 1.3 Is there "substantial investment"? — Yes, and this cuts against you
docs.text:
There's a well-known escape hatch here that does not apply. In BHB and OPAP the CJEU held that investment in creating data doesn't count — only investment in obtaining it, i.e. "the resources used to seek out existing independent materials and collect them in the database" (C‑203/02, summary point 1). That is why the horseracing board lost: they created the fixture data themselves.

Springer and Tebby did the opposite. They did not measure a single shift; they trawled thousands of primary papers (the derived dataset cites 3,648 references at v1, 6,853 at v3) and collected the values. That is the paradigm case of "obtaining." So unlike BHB, the substantial-investment limb is likely satisfied for both books. No help here.

docs.title: 1.4 Term — and this is where the case actually turns
docs.text:
Sui generis protection lasts 15 years, not 70. §87d UrhG: "Die Rechte des Datenbankherstellers erlöschen fünfzehn Jahre nach der Veröffentlichung der Datenbank." Art. 10(1)–(2) is the same.

Tebby, Handbook of Phosphorus-31 NMR Data, CRC Press, 1991 — the source of 6,608 of your 11,722 3D structures:

  • §137g(2) UrhG: for databases made between 1 Jan 1983 and 31 Dec 1997, "Die Schutzfrist beginnt in diesen Fällen am 1. Januar 1998." Fifteen years from 1 Jan 1998 → expired 31 December 2012. (Art. 14(3)/(5) of the Directive is to the same effect.)
  • Independently, Art. 11 limits the right to makers who are EU nationals/residents or EU-formed companies. CRC Press is Boca Raton, Florida. Art. 11(3) allows the Council to extend protection to third countries by agreement, and Recital 56 conditions it on reciprocity. [UNVERIFIED: I could not retrieve a Council decision under Art. 11(3) covering the US. My searching surfaced only a reference to an Isle of Man arrangement, which I did not retrieve or confirm. Treat the "no US extension" point as probable but unconfirmed — the term point above is the solid one and does not depend on it.]

Landolt-Börnstein III/40H, Springer, 2013/2014 — the source of 5,114 structures. The Ilm-NMR paper itself dates it: it digitised the Landolt-Börnstein "from 2014" (J. Cheminform. 2023, Methods; the cited reference is Gupta, Lechner, Kumar et al., vol. 40, Springer, 2013). Springer-Verlag is German, so Art. 11 is satisfied. Term runs to roughly the end of 2028 or 2029. This one is live, and 5,114 structures out of a 2,713 + 1,596 + 805 breakdown is plainly a substantial part both quantitatively (it is the bulk of those subvolumes' 3D- representable content) and qualitatively — BHB defines the qualitative test as "the scale of the investment in the obtaining, verification or presentation of the contents ... regardless of whether that subject represents a quantitatively substantial part" (C‑203/02, summary point 3).

One more trap worth knowing: §87a(1) sentence 2 — a database "wesentlich geänderte" counts as a new database with a fresh 15-year term, if the change required substantial investment (Art. 10(3) likewise). So a revised Landolt-Börnstein subvolume would restart the clock. Worth checking whether III/40H has been revised since 2014.

docs.title: 1.5 Copyright in the compilation — a separate, weaker claim
docs.text:
Distinct from the database right, §4 UrhG protects a Sammelwerk where "die Auswahl oder Anordnung der Elemente eine persönliche geistige Schöpfung" is — for 70 years post mortem auctoris. But it protects only the selection or arrangement, expressly "unbeschadet eines an den einzelnen Elementen gegebenenfalls bestehenden Urheberrechts".

The Ilm-NMR authors have a decent answer to this: per the paper's Methods, they re-drew every structure by hand in ACD/ChemSketch, generated their own SMILES, their own IDs and their own schema. They took the values, not the presentation. Whether taking the entire selection is itself an infringement of the selection is the arguable residue, and it is genuinely arguable — but it is a weaker claim than the database right and I would not expect it to be the thing that bites.

docs.title: 1.6 The TDM exceptions do not cover you — this is clear
docs.text:
This is the argument people reach for and it does not work.

§44b UrhG (implementing DSM Art. 4) permits "Vervielfältigungen von rechtmäßig zugänglichen Werken für das Text und Data Mining" — reproductions only. It says nothing about distribution or making available. It also requires deletion once no longer needed ("Die Vervielfältigungen sind zu löschen, wenn sie für das Text und Data Mining nicht mehr erforderlich sind") and is subject to machine-readable opt-out (§44b(3)). §87c(1) Nr. 4 extends it to substantial parts of databases — again, reproduction only.

§60d UrhG (DSM Art. 3) is broader for research organisations and does permit making copies available — but only "einem bestimmt abgegrenzten Kreis von Personen für deren gemeinsame wissenschaftliche Forschung" and to individual third parties for quality verification, and it must stop when the research concludes (§60d(4)).

Neither of these authorises publishing a corpus on PyPI and a public Nextcloud to an unbounded worldwide audience. The TDM exceptions let you train a model on the data. They do not let you ship the data. ChemMatData's entire product is shipping the data.

(Also note DSM Art. 7(1): contractual terms overriding the Art. 3 research exception are unenforceable — helpful for your own mining, irrelevant to redistribution.)

docs.title: 1.7 Good-faith reliance — helps with damages, not with an injunction
docs.text:
Under the database right, infringement does not require knowledge. What good faith affects is remedies, and §97 UrhG splits them cleanly. §97(1) gives removal and injunctive relief against anyone who "das Urheberrecht oder ein anderes nach diesem Gesetz geschütztes Recht widerrechtlich verletzt" — unlawfulness only, no fault required, and it extends to a first threatened infringement. §97(2) gives damages only against someone who acts "vorsätzlich oder fahrlässig". So:

  • Takedown / injunction: available against you even if you acted in perfect good faith.
  • Damages: require fault. Reliance on a facially valid CC-BY grant from a peer-reviewed J. Cheminformatics paper is decent evidence against negligence.
  • But: this memo destroys that. Once you have read an analysis saying the shifts came out of a 2014 Springer reference work with no documented permission, you have actual knowledge, and the good-faith argument for future distribution is gone. That is an unwelcome consequence of asking the question, and I'd rather say it than not.

GS Media (C‑160/15) does make knowledge and profit-motive decisive — but it is a copyright case about communication to the public under Art. 3(1) of Directive 2001/29, not a database-right case. Do not assume its knowledge test transfers to §87b.

docs.title: 1.8 The US contrast — the same act is lawful there
docs.text:
Feist killed "sweat of the brow" outright: the doctrine's "most glaring" flaw was that "it extended copyright protection in a compilation beyond selection and arrangement — the compiler's original contributions — to the facts themselves," which "eschewed the most fundamental axiom of copyright law" (499 U.S. 340). US compilations get only thin protection in original selection/arrangement, per 17 U.S.C. §103(b), and there is no US sui generis database right — Congress considered database bills in the late 1990s/2000s and none passed. [UNVERIFIED: I did not retrieve legislative history for the failed database bills; the absence of a federal database right is however evident from the Feist framework and from the Directive's own Recital 56 reciprocity condition, which would be pointless if the US had an equivalent.]

Concretely: a US-based maintainer redistributing the Ilm-NMR shift values, including the Landolt-Börnstein-derived ones, is doing something lawful. You, in Germany, hosting on a German Nextcloud, are not in the same position for the Landolt-Börnstein subset. Liability follows where you act, not where your users are — so a worldwide user base does not dilute your exposure, and your US users' lawful downloads do not launder your distribution.

docs.title: 2. Question 2(a): does linking change the legal position?
docs.text:
Extraction: yes, avoided. Art. 7(2)(a) requires "the permanent or temporary transfer of all or a substantial part of the contents ... to another medium". If no bytes touch your server, you don't transfer. (Note Directmedia, C‑304/07, holds that even manual on-screen consultation followed by re-keying is capable of being extraction — so this is narrower than it sounds, but the no-hosting version does escape it.)

Re-utilisation: no, not avoided. This is where the proposal fails.

Innoweb is the case on point, and it is close to fatal. The Court held that the operator of a dedicated meta search engine re-utilises the database, reasoning that:

"the relevant aspect of the activity of the operator ... — that is to say, making that search engine available on the Internet — comes close to the manufacture of a parasitical competing product ..., albeit without copying the information stored in the database concerned. In view of the search options offered, such a dedicated meta search engine resembles a database, but without having any data itself." (para 48)

And on timing — which kills the "but the user does the downloading" defence:

"actions actually carried out by the operator ... occur prior to activities carried out by end users and before a search is made in response to a given query. Such actions consist in making a dedicated meta search engine available on the Internet..." (para 29)

The operator's act is complete when the mechanism ships. That is pip install chem_mat_database.

CV-Online (C‑762/19) then dismissed the "but it's just a link" framing directly: hyperlinks and meta tags "are merely external manifestations, of secondary importance, of that extraction and that re-utilisation" (para 37).

Why Svensson doesn't rescue this. Svensson holds that "the provision on a website of clickable links to works freely available on another website does not constitute an 'act of communication to the public'" (C‑466/12, operative part). That is a copyright holding under Art. 3(1) of Directive 2001/29. It is not a holding about Art. 7 of Directive 96/9, and Innoweb — decided two months earlier — reaches the opposite result on the database right for functionally similar conduct. The two coexist because they concern different rights. Anyone telling you "linking is always fine, see Svensson" is conflating them.

The one authority that genuinely helps you is Renckhoff, and it is worth understanding why. The Court distinguished linking from re-hosting precisely on control:

"As regards the act of communication constituted by the posting on a website of a hyperlink ..., the preventive nature of the rights of the holder are preserved, since it is open to the author, if he no longer wishes to communicate his work on the website concerned, to remove it ..., rendering obsolete any hyperlink leading to it. However ... the posting on another website of a work gives rise to a new communication, independent of the communication initially authorised." (C‑161/17, para 44)

That is a real difference and it is in your favour on the copyright layer: if Springer ever forced a takedown at Zenodo, a link-based loader would go dark automatically, whereas your Nextcloud copy would not. It does not, however, answer the database-right point.

Caching on the user's machine does not change the operator's position. The user may have their own §44b defence for their own copy; you don't inherit it, and per Innoweb para 29 your act completed before theirs began.

Shipping the processing recipe alongside makes it worse, not better. Innoweb's first limb is whether the tool "provides the end user with a search form which essentially offers the same range of functionality as ... the database site". A loader that fetches the raw Zenodo archive and applies your curation, filtering and featurisation offers materially more functionality than the source. You would be arguing that you're less of a re-utiliser than Innoweb while shipping a strictly more capable product.

docs.title: The genuinely open question
docs.text:
CV-Online did not stop at "this is re-utilisation." It made harm a condition:

re-utilisation "may be prohibited by the maker of such a database where those acts adversely affect its investment ..., namely that they constitute a risk to the possibility of redeeming that investment through the normal operation of the database in question" (operative part)

and the Court framed the exercise as striking "a fair balance" between makers redeeming investment and "that of users and competitors ... in having access to the information ... and the possibility of creating innovative products based on that information" (para 140).

Both Innoweb and CV-Online involved commercial products that diverted advertising revenue from a competitor. A non-commercial academic loader that sends users to Zenodo — where Springer earns nothing either way — is a long way from that fact pattern. Nobody has litigated whether the harm condition is met when the "maker" whose investment is at risk is two hops upstream of the resource being linked, and when the linker is non-commercial.

That is the untested question, and it is the one worth putting to the legal office. My reading is that ChemMatData has a real argument on the harm limb and a poor one on the "is it re-utilisation at all" limb — which means the linking scheme buys you a defence, not safety, at a large engineering cost.

docs.title: 3. Question 2(b): engineering viability
docs.text: I read main.py, cache.py, dataset.py, web.py, config.py, connectors.py and cli.py in the worktree. This is a structural change, not a small one. Six specific reasons.

docs.title: 3.1 The load path has exactly one source model
docs.text: load_graph_dataset / load_smiles_dataset / load_xyz_dataset all funnel into chem_mat_data/main.py:77 ensure_dataset(), which does: local file → config.cache → web.py:NextcloudFileShare. web.py:269 construct_download_url() hard-codes a Nextcloud WebDAV path ({base_url}/public.php/dav/files/{share_token}/{file_name}), and ensure_dataset assumes one file per dataset per extension with a .gz/.zip fallback ladder. There is a FILE_SHARE_CLASS_MAP in main.py:26 but it has exactly one entry ('nextcloud'), and metadata.yml is fetched from the same share to decide what exists at all (main.py:145). A per-dataset source override is new plumbing through all of it.

docs.title: 3.2 ZenodoSource exists — but only at build time
docs.text:
connectors.py has ZenodoSource, FigshareSource and FileDownloadSource. Grepping for importers: every one is a chem_mat_data/scripts/create_graph_datasets__*.py plus tests/test_connectors.py. Nothing in the user-facing load path imports connectors at all. That separation is currently doing real work — it's the line between "maintainer's machine, once" and "user's machine, every time." The proposal erases it.

ZenodoSource also isn't built for this. prepare() does tempfile.mkdtemp(), fetch() downloads the whole archive and extracts it, and cleanup() runs from __del__. It is deliberately ephemeral and has no Cache integration whatsoever. On the code as it stands, every single load re-downloads the whole archive.

docs.title: 3.3 The cache cannot express versions
docs.text: cache.py:171 construct_base_name() returns f'{name}.{typ}'. That is the entire cache key. No version, no checksum, no source URL. Two different Zenodo versions of Ilm-NMR-P31 would occupy the same slot with nothing to distinguish them, and contains_dataset() (cache.py:21) checks only whether the .yml exists — so a stale v2.0 cache entry would satisfy a v3.0 request silently. Adding version-awareness means changing the key format, which invalidates every existing user's cache.

docs.title: 3.4 Reproducibility: this record is a moving target
docs.text:
I queried the Zenodo API. The concept record is 8260782; there are five versions in under three years:

Record DOI Version Published Files 8260783 10.5281/zenodo.8260783 1.0 2023-08-18 4 15658468 10.5281/zenodo.15658468 2.0 2025-06-13 5 17649620 10.5281/zenodo.17649620 2.1 2025-11-19 5 17952686 10.5281/zenodo.17952686 2.2 2025-12-17 5 20762603 10.5281/zenodo.20762603 3.0 2026-06-19 5

The content is not stable in any sense that matters:

  • Entry count went 14,250 → 43,317; molecules 13,730 → 39,107; references 3,648 → 6,853.
  • xyz_nmr_data.zip did not exist before v2.0. The 3D geometries you want appeared in June 2025, then grew 136.4 MB → 155.1 MB by v3.0.
  • v3.0 removed the origin column and changed the SDF NMREDATA_* tags.

So: a concept-DOI pin (10.5281/zenodo.8260782) always resolves to the newest version and would have silently swapped a 14k-molecule dataset for a 43k one under your users' feet, and would have broken any script reading origin. A versioned-DOI pin (20762603) is stable — but then you hand-re-pin on every upstream release, which is a maintenance burden you don't have today, and Zenodo depositors can restrict or withdraw old versions. Neither option is as reproducible as a frozen .mpack on your own share.

Note also that the paper cites 10.5281/zenodo.8260783 — the versioned DOI of v1.0. The v1.0 the paper describes doesn't even contain 3D coordinates.

docs.title: 3.5 It discards the entire point of the .mpack model
docs.text:
The value proposition of ChemMatData is that expensive processing happens once, centrally. load_graph_dataset is ensure_dataset(...) then load_graphs(file_path) — a msgpack deserialise into arrays. Fetch-at-load-time means every user instead:

  • downloads 155 MB (xyz_nmr_data.zip at v3.0) rather than a gzipped .mpack;
  • extracts it;
  • re-runs the RDKit parsing and featurisation in processing.py (56 KB) and the XyzDataset / GraphDataset path in dataset.py (53 KB);
  • and gets results that depend on their RDKit/OpenBabel versions.

That last one is the serious one. Today an RDKit change is your problem, absorbed once at build time. Under the proposal it becomes a silent per-user data divergence — the same load_xyz_dataset('ilm_nmr_p31') call returning different featurisations on different machines. To avoid that you'd have to pin and ship a reproducible processing environment, which is a much bigger commitment than a download path.

docs.title: 3.6 Offline use, rate limits, failure modes
docs.text:
Offline use currently works: main.py:112 returns early if the file is on disk, and main.py:124 consults the cache before any network call. A Zenodo-backed path is offline- capable only to the extent you build a cache for it — i.e. you re-implement the thing you already have, against a second backend.

You also inherit a dependency you don't control: Zenodo availability, Zenodo's rate limits (a CI matrix or a lecture hall behind one NAT is a realistic trigger) [UNVERIFIED: I did not fetch Zenodo's current published rate-limit figures, so treat the severity as unquantified — the dependency itself is certain, the thresholds are not], and per-file URLs that change shape between record versions. ZenodoSource.fetch() currently does a bare requests.get(..., stream=True) with raise_for_status() and no retry, no backoff, no resume, no checksum verification — for a 155 MB download.

docs.title: Verdict
docs.text: Small change: adding a source: field to metadata.yml and a build-time connector. You already have that. Structural change: making the user's load path fetch from arbitrary third-party repositories, with a version-aware cache, a pinned client-side processing environment, and a second failure domain. That is the one being proposed, and it buys a legal defence that Innoweb and CV-Online suggest is weak anyway.

docs.title: 4. The option nobody has proposed
docs.text:
The framing so far has been all-or-nothing: ship everything, or ship nothing, or link. The term analysis in §1.4 opens a fourth door.

Ship the HBP-derived subset. Hold back the Landolt-Börnstein-derived subset until 2029.

  • HBP (Tebby / CRC Press, 1991): 6,608 structures — 56% of your 3D data. The German database right expired 31 Dec 2012 under §137g(2) UrhG. The values were never protected as such. The compilation-copyright claim on selection/arrangement is weak given that the Ilm-NMR authors re-drew every structure and built their own schema. This block is on firm ground.
  • Lan1/2/3 (Landolt-Börnstein / Springer, 2013/14): 5,114 structures. Live database right until ~2029. This is the block to hold, or to get permission for.

You said the 3D subset "is 100% book-derived and cannot be filtered clean" — which is true as stated, but the two books are not in the same legal position, and the dataset distinguishes them. Your own count is broken out by source (HBP 6,608; Lan1 2,713; Lan2 1,596; Lan3 805), so the filter is a source column predicate, not a research project.

A 6,608-structure ³¹P dataset with DFT geometries is still a genuinely useful public resource, and it ships now instead of in three years.

In parallel, ask Springer. A written permission request to Springer Nature for use of Landolt-Börnstein III/40H-derived shift values in a non-commercial academic ML dataset is not an outlandish ask, it costs one email, and a "yes" resolves the whole question. It is also worth telling the Ilm-NMR authors what you found — they may already hold a permission that simply isn't documented in the paper, which would collapse this entire analysis.

docs.title: 5. A general rule for the collection
docs.text: Proposed addition to .claude/skills/dataset-extraction/references/license.md. It extends the existing "Trap 1 — the upstream database" section, which already gets the principle right but stops one step short.

docs.title: 5.1 The rule
docs.text:
A dataset's licence describes the last link in its provenance chain. Your right to redistribute is determined by the most restrictive link, not the last one.

Every compiled dataset has a chain: primary measurement → some compilation → possibly another compilation → the record you found. A CC-BY tag on the final record binds only the rights that depositor actually held. CC BY 4.0 §1(7) limits the grant to rights "that the Licensor has authority to license", and §5(a) disclaims any warranty of title — the licence itself tells you it is not a guarantee.

docs.title: 5.2 The classification
docs.text:
Add a BLOCK tier. The current table has only PASS and ESCALATE, which forces genuinely unshippable cases into the same bucket as merely-awkward ones.

Verdict Trigger BLOCK Data digitised or scraped from a commercially sold reference work, database or journal corpus, where (a) no publisher permission is documented, and (b) the source was published within the last 15 years, and (c) the source publisher is EU/EEA-based. All three must hold. ESCALATE Any two of (a)/(b)/(c). Also: everything already in the existing ESCALATE row (NC, SA, copyleft, bespoke terms, no licence stated). Also: an upstream reference work more than 15 years old where the selection is being taken wholesale rather than the values. PASS Upstream is primary literature, a public database with permissive terms, the depositor's own measurements or computations, or a compilation whose sui generis term has expired and whose values are being taken rather than its arrangement.

docs.title: 5.3 Three new manifest fields
docs.text:
The existing upstream_database / upstream_terms_url / upstream_license fields cannot express any of the above. Add:

{
  "upstream_publication_year": 2014,
  "upstream_publisher_jurisdiction": "DE",
  "upstream_is_commercial_product": true
}

These are cheap to establish (they're on the book's copyright page) and they mechanise the BLOCK/ESCALATE decision instead of leaving it to judgement at the point where, as license.md already observes, "an ambiguous license gets read charitably."

docs.title: 5.4 Two rules of thumb worth stating flatly
docs.text:
• "It's already public" is never an answer. Publication by a third party is not a grant. Nor is "everyone else uses this dataset." The existing file says this about missing licences; it should say it about upstream rights too, which is the harder case.
  • Linking is not a workaround. If a dataset would be BLOCKed when hosted, it is BLOCKed when fetched at load time. Innoweb para 48 and CV-Online para 37 are the reason. Record this so that the next person to have this idea finds the answer instead of re-deriving it.

docs.title: 5.5 One structural gap
docs.text:
metadata.yml has 46 datasets and no licence field at all. The keys in use are: compounds, description, raw, tags, target_type, targets, verbose, sources, target_descriptions, full, notes, category, min_version. sources is free text and appears on 36 of 46.

So the skill's licence gate produces a finding that is then discarded — it lives in .dataset_work/<slug>/manifest.yml and never reaches the shipped metadata or the user. A license: block in metadata.yml, surfaced by cmdata info, would mean attribution obligations actually travel with the data (which CC-BY §3(a) requires of you when you Share) and that any future problem is auditable across the collection rather than one dataset at a time. That is a small change with a large payoff, and it is worth doing regardless of how Ilm-NMR-P31 is resolved.

docs.title: 6. What to ask the legal office
docs.text:
Not "is this OK". These:

  1. Term and beneficiary. Do you agree the Tebby/CRC 1991 handbook's sui generis right expired 31 Dec 2012 under §137g(2) UrhG, and that as a US-made database it likely never attracted the right under §87e-relevant Art. 11 in the first place? If so, is redistributing the 6,608 HBP-derived structures acceptable, given that the shift values themselves are unprotected facts?
  2. The live block. For the 5,114 Landolt-Börnstein-derived structures (Springer, 2013/14): do you regard that as a substantial part of the III/40H subvolumes under §87b? And has III/40H been substantially revised since 2014 in a way that would restart the term under §87a(1) sentence 2?
  3. Compilation copyright. Independently of the database right — the Ilm-NMR authors re-drew all structures and built their own schema, taking values but not arrangement. Is that sufficient to avoid §4 UrhG Sammelwerk copyright, which would otherwise run for 70 years p.m.a. and would outlast the database right by decades?
  4. Downstream position. ChemMatData relies on a CC-BY-4.0 grant from a peer-reviewed publication. Given CC BY §1(7) ("rights ... that the Licensor has authority to license") and §5(a)'s disclaimer of title, what is KIT's exposure if the grant is partly invalid — and does the analysis change now that we have actual knowledge of the provenance?
  5. The linking question. Does Innoweb (C‑202/12, esp. para 48) combined with CV-Online (C‑762/19, para 37) mean that shipping a client that fetches from Zenodo at load time is "re-utilisation" under §87b, notwithstanding that no data sits on our server? And does CV-Online's harm-to-investment condition offer a real defence for a non-commercial academic tool where the upstream maker is two hops removed?
  6. Institutional posture. Does KIT want a standing policy for this class of case, given it will recur across the collection? Specifically: is the BLOCK criterion in §5.2 above (commercial + within 15 years + EU publisher, no permission) one legal is comfortable endorsing as an automated gate?
  7. Practical. Is there an institutional route for a permission request to Springer Nature for Landolt-Börnstein-derived values in a non-commercial ML dataset, and would legal prefer to send it?

docs.title: 7. What I could not establish
docs.text:
• Whether any Council agreement under Art. 11(3) of Directive 96/9/EC extends the sui generis right to US-made databases. Searching surfaced a reference to an Isle of Man arrangement which I did not retrieve. The Tebby conclusion does not depend on this — the term expiry under §137g(2) is independently decisive — but the Art. 11 argument is unconfirmed.
  • Whether Landolt-Börnstein III/40H has been substantially revised since 2014. If it has, §87a(1) sentence 2 restarts a fresh 15-year term and pushes the block past 2029. Checkable from Springer's catalogue; I did not.
  • The actual licence terms under which the Ilm-NMR authors obtained the Landolt-Börnstein and CRC PDFs. The paper says both "are available as PDF documents and could thus partially be read by machines," which implies institutional subscription access. Springer and CRC subscription agreements routinely contain TDM and redistribution clauses that would govern independently of copyright — a contractual restriction that no statutory analysis above touches. I could not see those agreements. This may matter more than everything above, because contract can bind where copyright does not.
  • Whether the Ilm-NMR authors in fact hold permission. Absent from the paper, but absence of documentation is not documentation of absence. Worth one email.
  • German case law on printed reference works as Datenbanken under §87a. I relied on Art. 1(2)'s "or other means" and the CJEU's broad definition in OPAP; I did not retrieve a German decision squarely on a printed scientific reference table.
  • Zenodo's current published rate limits. The runtime dependency is certain; the thresholds are unquantified here.
  • No US case law is cited beyond Feist. I did not attempt to find US authority on scientific-data compilations specifically, and the "no federal database right" statement rests on the Feist framework rather than on retrieved legislative history.

docs.title: dataset-search: what to fix next, ranked
docs.text:
Scope: the skill at .claude/skills/dataset-search/ (735 lines across SKILL.md, references/sweep.md, references/verification.md, references/bookkeeping.md), chem_mat_data/discovery/ledger.py, and the discover check / discover verdict commands in chem_mat_data/manage.py. All line numbers are against b336db6 on master.

Method, and what the method does not cover. Four review lenses ran over the skill — simulate (walk a run start to finish), contract (does the prose match what the code does), design (is the arrangement right), failure (what happens when a step goes wrong). Each lens was capped at its four strongest findings. Eleven findings reached an independent skeptic whose job was to refute them; seven survived, four were refuted. The seven collapse to five distinct defects, because three lenses independently found the MISSING_DATASETS.md gap and two found the subagent-budget mismatch. The cap is a cap and not a clean bill: every lens that returned four had weaker findings it could not report, so absence from this list is not evidence of absence.

Where the skeptic supplied a correction, the corrected version is what appears below, and the correction is named.

No live sweep was exercised. Outbound HTTPS from Python fails in the review environment with a self-signed-certificate error (a TLS-intercepting proxy), so discover stream, fetch and score were never run. Everything below was established against the 1000-record discovery_stream.csv already on disk, the CLI, the ledger module, and isolated reproductions in a scratch directory. Nothing in this document depends on network behaviour.

docs.title: The structural conclusion
docs.text:
Every defect below sits on the same seam: the skill reasons about one run, and the machinery it drives keeps state across all runs.

  • The budget line counts this sweep's flags; the screen returns every sweep's unjudged flags (finding 5).
  • --include-title adds a column to a CSV that earlier runs already wrote a header for (finding 1).
  • MISSING_DATASETS.md accumulates across runs and is the one cross-run file nothing screens against (finding 3).
  • The verdict ledger is the cross-run memory, and nothing checks that this run finished writing to it (finding 4).
  • --force is the only cross-run correction channel the tool advertises, and it is inert (finding 2).

Design decision 2 — no gates, state lives in files — is upheld by this review, and three of the five fixes are one or two sentences of prose. But the state that lives in files is shared state, and the skill currently documents it as though each run owned it. That is the single edit that would prevent the next four findings of this shape.

None of the nine stated design decisions was overturned. Five were attacked and all five held: licensing out of scope (5), downloadability not required (6), the shared sweep ledger (8, attacked twice), no gate machinery (2), and no input / unattended runs (1). Two proposals were rejected because they would have broken a decision that is correct — see the tail section, and the "do not do this" clauses in findings 3 and 5.

docs.title: Defects
docs.text: Ranked by severity. These are bugs and gaps; act on them directly.

docs.title: 1. discover check never shows a title, and --include-title makes the shared ledger ragged
docs.text:
Anchor: .claude/skills/dataset-search/SKILL.md:100, chem_mat_data/manage.py:3020. Lenses: simulate, contract. Severity: high (on your machine; medium on a fresh clone).

Two separable defects that meet in the same flag.

(a) No output of discover check carries a title. SKILL.md:100 says --include-title is worth taking because "the screening report and the subagent briefs both read better with titles than with bare DOIs". The --from-csv loop (manage.py:3343-3346) reads row['flagged'] and row['url'] and nothing else, so the title is discarded at ingestion; ScreenResult.to_dict() (ledger.py:481) emits url/status/detail/source/skip; the Rich table prints status, url, matched; --new-only echoes the URL. I ran cmmanage discover check --from-csv discovery_stream.csv and --json — no title in any mode, on any checkout. So screening.txt has no titles, and stage 3's "Give each subagent the paper's title, its URL, and this task" (SKILL.md:166, repeated at verification.md:64) names an input no upstream stage hands over. The agent must invent an unprompted join back to the CSV.

(b) That join is broken on this machine, and the flag is what breaks it. discovery_stream.csv here has the five-column header openalex_id,url,score,flagged,publication_year and 1000 rows. discover stream resumes by default; on an existing non-empty file it sets write_header = False (manage.py:3028) while columns has already gained title (manage.py:3020), and opens the file in append mode (manage.py:3083). The first run of this skill therefore appends six-field rows under a five-field header. pd.read_csv on the result raises ParserError; csv.DictReader strands the title under the None restkey. Screening itself keeps working, because flagged and url sit before the ragged field.

Scope, per the skeptic's correction. git check-ignore -v discovery_stream.csv → .gitignore:47:*.csv, so nothing ships and a fresh clone writes a correct six-column header. (b) is a migration case — and the machine it bites is yours, with exactly that five-column file, on the first invocation. The skeptic also lowered (a) from blocking to degrading: the subagent resolves the URL regardless and returns the title in its report, so candidates.md can be titled from the reports. What (a) costs is brief readability and parent-side bookkeeping, not verification.

Not pinned by any test. grep title over both named test files returns nothing, and tests/test_discovery_stream.py:104 tests the row-building function on a fresh record — the resume-plus---include-title path through the CSV writer is untested.

Change. (a) Carry title through discover check --from-csv: into the --json dicts, as a column in the table, and after the URL in --new-only. (b) Make discover stream compare its column set against an existing file's header and exit with a message naming --include-title — "discovery_stream.csv has no title column; re-run without --include-title or start a new --out" — rather than appending a differently shaped row. (c) Until (a) lands, drop the "screening report" half of SKILL.md:100 and say where stage 3 is supposed to get the title from.

docs.title: 2. verdict --force reports success for a correction that changes nothing
docs.text:
Anchor: chem_mat_data/discovery/ledger.py:379. Lenses: contract, failure. Severity: medium.

VerdictLedger._index does self._by_key.setdefault(key, verdict), and load() appends rows in file order, so the earliest row for a URL is what lookup returns forever — and append() re-indexes in-process, so the correction is invisible without even a reload. STATUS_VERIFIED is in SKIP_STATUSES (ledger.py:73) whatever the decision was.

Reproduced in an isolated ledger: append unclear with why='ACS bot check', then append confirmed/foo_db for the same URL. Two rows land on disk; screen_many returns verified | unclear | skip True. The corrected row is in the committed file and is unreachable.

Meanwhile cmmanage discover verdict --help advertises --force Append even though this paper already has a verdict, and the duplicate refusal path prints "pass --force to append a second verdict for the same paper". An agent or human that hits the refusal is pointed by the tool at a flag that does nothing, gets OK recorded confirmed for it, and moves on. grep -rn -- --force .claude/skills/dataset-search/ returns nothing — the skill never mentions the flag at all.

The skeptic's correction, and it matters. Do not read this as "an unclear buries a paper". Burial is deliberate and correct: verification.md:105 says outright that "unclear is a real answer and recording it is what stops the next sweep from re-verifying the same unreachable paper." What is not deliberate is that the only correction channel the tool offers is a silent no-op. The trigger is narrow — screening drops settled papers before stage 3, so the skill's own loop never revisits an unclear; you need a human-initiated recheck, an in-run recovery after a subagent failure, or a maintainer fixing the ledger by hand. Narrow, but entirely foreseeable, and silent success is the worst failure class in a skill whose whole economy is "never re-verify a settled paper".

Not pinned: tests/test_discovery_ledger.py:359 (test_verdict_refuses_a_duplicate_and_quotes_the_prior_reason) asserts only forced.exit_code == 0. It never asserts which verdict wins afterwards.

Change. Make the last verdict win: self._by_key[key] = verdict at ledger.py:379. Rows carry a date and the file is append-only, so file order is the intended precedence. Keep the duplicate refusal so --force stays a deliberate act. Then add to SKILL.md's recording section what --force now means: "discover verdict refuses a paper that already has a verdict and quotes the prior reason. To supersede one — you reached a page an earlier run recorded as unclear — re-run with --force; the newer row wins."

If you want first-wins to stand instead, the equivalent fix is to make --force say so: refuse it, or print "recorded as an annotation; screening still returns the earlier <decision> — hand-edit docs/search_verdicts.md to supersede". Silently succeeding is the part that cannot stay either way.

Risk. Last-write-wins over an append-only log is the natural semantics; the only cross-key interaction is _keys_for(record_url), and check is only ever fed paper URLs (arguments, or the url column of the stream CSV), so a later row's record_url cannot shadow an unrelated paper's screening result.

docs.title: 3. MISSING_DATASETS.md is written but never screened, and promotion has no duplicate check
docs.text:
Anchor: .claude/skills/dataset-search/SKILL.md:231, chem_mat_data/discovery/ledger.py:492. Lenses: contract, design, failure (all three found it independently). Severity: medium.

screen_many (ledger.py:492-538) consults exactly three sources: load_rejected(), load_catalog(), VerdictLedger.load(). MISSING_DATASETS.md is not among them, and bookkeeping.md:13 states the read-only set as metadata.yml plus rejected_datasets.md. The file holds 77 distinct DOIs across 86 numbered rows — the largest store of already-known leads in the repository, and the file this skill writes into.

Verified: cmmanage discover check --json 'https://doi.org/10.1039/D4DD00196F' 'https://doi.org/10.1186/s13321-019-0384-1' returns "status": "new", "skip": false for both. Those are rows 3 (Polyuniverse) and 7 (pKa QSAR) of MISSING_DATASETS.md. The promotion instruction (SKILL.md:231-241, bookkeeping.md:73-76) says only "Append to the table that fits… continue the numbering" — there is no instruction anywhere to check whether the row already exists. verification.md:136-139 handles preprint-versus-published duplicates within a run and nothing else.

When it fires. discover stream defaults to --year-min 2010 and sorts publication_year:desc, so ordinary continued pagination walks back into the years the leads come from. Today's flagged set does not overlap (0 of 115) only because discovery_stream.csv currently holds nothing but 2025 and 2026 records while the leads span 2003-2025. --year-min 2005 (sweep.md:105) widens it further. The cursor-reset remedy (sweep.md:107) is not the trigger — .ids is deliberately preserved there. The leads are also the classifier's own training positives, so they score high and get flagged when reached.

Consequence. One wasted verification subagent per re-encountered lead, plus a duplicate row appended to a committed file under a fresh number. Bounded, not progressive: the same run records a verdict, after which the paper screens verified forever, so the ceiling is roughly 77 subagents and 77 duplicate rows, once. The duplicate rows are the part that persists — the next person picking a lead cannot tell them from new ones.

Change, and note that the skeptic reversed the direction here. Do not add MISSING_DATASETS.md as a fourth skip-ledger. Those rows are not decisions the way rejected / in_catalog / verified are: _identify_positives.py:23 confirmed them with identify_dataset(title) — an LLM call on the title alone, no abstract, no paper fetch, no data-record visit — and POSITIVES_VALIDATION.md:97 measured 26% label noise on that same population ("Of 142 entries, 37 were rejected by the agent"). Skipping them would permanently entrench title-only guesses and deny them the record_url and entry counts that only a verify subagent produces and that /dataset-extraction consumes.

Do this instead: (a) SKILL.md:231 — before appending, grep the candidate's DOI against MISSING_DATASETS.md. On a hit, update that row in place with the record URL and entry counts the subagent found, rather than adding a second row, and say so in findings.md. That turns a re-discovery from a duplicate into an enrichment of a weakly-sourced lead. (b) Amend SKILL.md:136 and bookkeeping.md:85-99 to name both blind spots. Today they name only the 13-of-46 catalog sources gap, which reads as exhaustive. (c) Optional, and the better version of the code change: report a MISSING_DATASETS.md hit as a non-skipping status (listed, outside SKIP_STATUSES), so the agent is told rather than having to remember to grep. The paper still gets verified and still gets a real verdict.

Also fix the numbering instruction while you are there: "continue the numbering" is undefined against a file whose numbers are non-contiguous upstream indices interleaved across five sections, with a global maximum of 142 over 86 rows. Say "continue from the global maximum across all sections".

docs.title: 4. Nothing checks that the verdict ledger is complete when the run ends
docs.text:
Anchor: .claude/skills/dataset-search/SKILL.md:254. Lens: design. Severity: medium.

SKILL.md:282: "There is no manifest and no gates here; the state is the files." The one command that would close the loop — cmmanage discover check --from-csv discovery_stream.csv --new-only — appears at stage 2 (SKILL.md:121) and under Resuming (SKILL.md:288, "That last command is the resume point"), but never at the end of stage 4. Stage 4 ends at "Then tell the user: how many papers were swept, how many verified…" with the count coming from the agent's own memory. Every stage-4 deliverable — candidates.md, findings.md, the promoted rows — can be written correctly whether or not discover verdict was ever called.

Two ways a verdict goes missing: a batch that returns while the agent is writing candidates.md, and an unclear the agent means to come back to. (The skeptic removed a third mechanism the finding originally claimed: a verdict that exits 1 on a duplicate cannot leave a gap, because the refusal only fires when lookup already matched a key, and _index registers both url and record_url into the same map screen_many reads.)

The skeptic also added the failure that makes this check worth more than a compliance nag. _keys_for mints a doi: key only when the string literally contains a 10.dddd/… DOI. I ran it:

_keys_for('https://www.nature.com/articles/s41597-023-02123-4')
  -> {'url:nature.com/articles/s41597-023-02123-4'}
_keys_for('https://doi.org/10.1038/s41597-023-02123-4')
  -> {'doi:10.1038/s41597-023-02123-4', 'url:doi.org/10.1038/s41597-023-02123-4'}

The CSV row for that paper is the doi.org form. So a verdict recorded exactly as instructed — under the resolved publisher URL the subagent reported — is invisible to the next sweep. That is a silent ledger row no amount of care about remembering to record prevents.

Consequence. Bounded but silent: each dropped or mis-keyed verdict costs one re-verification on the next run, which is precisely the cost the whole design exists to avoid. It does not compound — the re-verification records a verdict — so the waste is roughly (drop rate × flagged papers) per run, not a growing backlog.

Change. (a) Close stage 4 with the command the skill already documents, run in the other direction: re-run cmmanage discover check --from-csv discovery_stream.csv --new-only, diff it against the list stage 2 produced, and require that every URL that was given a subagent has disappeared. Anything still printed is a verdict that was not recorded — record it now, or name it in findings.md as deliberately deferred. (b) Take the run report's "how many verified" from grep -c '^| http' docs/search_verdicts.md before and after, not from memory. (c) One line in stage 3: pass discover verdict the URL exactly as it appears in the CSV, not the resolved publisher URL the subagent reports.

This is the gate-equivalent, it costs milliseconds, and it introduces no gate machinery — design decision 2 stands. It is one command the skill already teaches, invoked one stage later.

docs.title: Design disagreement
docs.text: One finding. Act on it differently: the mechanism is correct and the prose is what is wrong, and the obvious "fix" would break a decision that is right.

docs.title: 5. The subagent budget counts this sweep's flags; stage 3's queue is every unjudged flag ever swept
docs.text:
Anchor: .claude/skills/dataset-search/SKILL.md:96-99. Lenses: simulate, contract, design, failure. Severity: medium.

SKILL.md:96-99: "At the flag rate this sweep actually produces — 115 of 1000, measured — 300 papers is about 35 flagged, which is about 35 subagents." Stage 2's working list is cmmanage discover check --from-csv discovery_stream.csv --new-only over a file that SKILL.md:90-94 and sweep.md:85-88 both insist stays shared and ever-growing, and check --help shows no row, limit, or year bound. So the working list is every flagged row across all sweeps that has never received a verdict.

Run today:

$ cmmanage discover check --from-csv discovery_stream.csv
… 115 checked - 115 new -> 115 worth verifying
$ grep -c '^| http' docs/search_verdicts.md
0

A bare invocation on this repository therefore hands stage 3 roughly 150 papers — the 115-row backlog plus this sweep's ~35 — after the skill told the reader to expect 35. The 115 is the residue of the one-off 1000-record measurement sweep whose flag rate SKILL.md:96 and sweep.md:61 both quote and which was never verified.

What is and is not wrong. The mechanism is right: in steady state the two numbers coincide, because every verified paper gets a verdict, and they diverge only when a sweep ran without verification or a run was interrupted. Nothing is stuck, either — the count is printed by the stage-2 command before any subagent exists, SKILL.md:142 already tells the agent to record it, and Resuming already frames outstanding new rows as the work left. discovery_stream.csv is gitignored, so a fresh clone sees 35. What is wrong is that the number a reader was promised is off by 4x on the author's own machine, with no sentence anywhere saying it could be.

Change — one clause each, no new flags. At SKILL.md:96-99: "…about 35 flagged from this sweep, plus any flagged rows earlier sweeps left unjudged — the number stage 2 prints is the real subagent count." At stage 2, after the --new-only command: "This is every flagged paper from every sweep that has never been given a verdict, not just this sweep's records. If it is far larger than this sweep's own flag count, an earlier sweep was never verified — say so in findings.md and tell the user the batch count before spawning." Optionally a fifth Escalation bullet: "discover check reports far more new papers than this sweep flagged — say the number and confirm before spawning."

Do not add --since-row, --tail or --limit to discover check, and do not screen only this run's rows. Both skeptics rejected it independently and for the same reason: it permanently orphans every flagged paper an interrupted or pre-skill run never judged, which is exactly what the shared sweep ledger plus the committed verdict ledger exist to recover, and it inverts the recall-first trade the 0.05 threshold was chosen for (sweep.md:62-63: "a false positive costs one subagent, a false negative loses a dataset permanently"). Do not add a blocking confirmation gate either — design decision 1 makes unattended runs deliberate; report the number, do not stop on it.

docs.title: Considered and rejected
docs.text:
Each of these was raised by a lens and refuted by the skeptic.

The subagent brief writes to a path built from values the skill refuses to give it (<run>, <openalex_id>). The parent has both: openalex_id is column 1 of discovery_stream.csv, the file stage 2 already reads. verification.md:64's "give it the title and the URL, nothing else" is a bias rule about what you may say about the paper — it cannot forbid the path, which sits inside the blockquote the parent hands over. The angle-bracket placeholder convention is used identically throughout both skills, including in /dataset-extraction's subagent briefs, which have survived real runs.

Most of what the sweep flags is a repository deposit, not an article, and the brief's first instruction does not apply. The OpenAlex filter is type:journal-article|proceedings-article|report plus has_abstract:true, so a bare deposit cannot reach the classifier. The flagged Zenodo rows resolve as type: report with full abstracts — Zenodo-published documents whose landing page is the publication page. verification.md:79, the first confirmed bullet, is "A Zenodo, Figshare, Dryad or institutional record with data files", which is exactly the rule said to be missing.

The promoted lead drops the record URL and the licence observation, and ranks on size alone. All three limbs are false. bookkeeping.md:128 explicitly puts the licence observation in the review file and the candidate's notes; --record-url is a column of docs/search_verdicts.md and is indexed for screening (ledger.py:378); the ranking rule names four criteria, not one, and bookkeeping.md:84 carries the access barrier into Data Type. A mandatory licence field on the search subagent would systematically capture the article licence and stamp it, ungated, onto a committed leads list — precisely the failure design decision 5 exists to prevent.

An interrupt between a batch returning and its verdicts being recorded loses the work, and the review files cannot be recovered because their filenames have no usable key. The filename key is the join key: awk -F, '$1=="W7153478152"{print $2}' discovery_stream.csv recovers the URL in one line. Verdicts are recorded as each subagent returns, so a resume at any batch boundary loses nothing, and Resuming's first two commands read the run directory. (The residual risk here is covered properly by finding 4.)
