docs.title: Command Line Interface (CLI)
docs.text: After installing the chem_mat_data package, you should have access to the cmdata command line interface which allows to interact with the remote file share server to, for example, list all the available datasets or to download them into a local directory.

docs.title: Help Option
docs.text:
You can use the --help option to get a list of all the available commands:

cmdata --help

docs.title: Simple Commands
docs.text:
To view a list of all the available datasets on the remote file share server, you can use the list command:

cmdata list

This command will produce a list view as shown below

You can then use the download command to download one of the datasets by using its unique string name:

cmdata download "clintox"

This command will, for example, download a raw clintox.csv file into the current working directory. This raw CSV dataset format consists of a list of SMILES molecule representations and their corresponding target value annotations - in this case a classification label of the molecules toxicity.

docs.title: Programming Interface (API)
docs.text: Alternatively, the chem_mat_data functionality can be used programmatically as part of python code. The package provides each dataset either in raw or processed/graph format (For further information on the distincation visit the Loading Datasets) documentation.

docs.title: Raw Datasets
docs.text:
You can use the load_smiles_dataset function to download the raw dataset format. This function will return the dataset as a pandas.DataFrame object which contains a "smiles" column along with the specific target value annotations as separate data frame columns.

import pandas as pd
from chem_mat_data import load_smiles_dataset

df: pd.DataFrame = load_smiles_dataset('clintox')
print(df.head())

docs.title: Graph Datasets
docs.text:
You can also use the load_graph_dataset function to download the same dataset in the pre-processed graph representation. This function will return a list of dict objects which contain the full graph representation of the corresponding molecules.

from rich.pretty import pprint
from chem_mat_data import load_graph_dataset

graphs: list[dict] = load_graph_dataset('clintox')
example_graph = graphs[0]
pprint(example_graph)

For more details on the structure of this graph representation, please refer to the Graph Representation documentation.

(Insert an example of how to train a PyG model with this representation)

docs.title: Graph Representation
docs.text: The chem_mat_data package provides various chemical property prediction datasets in a pre-processed format, in which molecules are mapped to graph structures that represent the atoms as nodes and the bonds as corresponding edges.

docs.title: Graph Dict Structure
docs.text:
Practically, this graph structure is represented as a native python dict object with a set of specific attributes.

Generally, the graph dict structure follows the following naming convention

  • Prefix node_ for node-level attributes with shape \((V, ?)\)
  • Prefix edge_ for edge-level attributes with shape \((E, ?)\)
  • Prefix graph_ for graph-level attributes with shape \((?, )\)

More specifically, each graph dict object has the following minimal set of attributes:

Attribute Description node_indices Integer numpy array of shape \((V, )\) where \(V\) is the number of nodes in the graph. Contains the unique integer indices of the graph nodes. node_attributes Float numpy array of shape \((V, N)\) where \(V\) is the number of nodes and \(N\) is the number of numeric node features. Contains the numeric feature vectors that represent each node. edge_indices Integer numpy array of shape \((E, 2)\) where \(E\) is the number of edges in the graph. Contains tuples \((i, j)\) of node indices that indicate the existence of an edge between nodes \(i\) and \(j\). edge_attributes Float numpy array of shape \((E, M)\) where \(E\) is the number of edges in the graph and \(M\) is the number of values in the graph. graph_labels Float numpy array of shape \((T, )\) where \(T\) is the number of target values associated with each element of the dataset. The target values can either be continuous regression targets such as [1.43, -9.4] or could be one-hot classification labels such as [0, 1, 0]. graph_repr The string numpy array of shape \((1, )\) containing the string SMILES representation of the original molecule.

Depending on the dataset, the graph dict representation may contain additional attributes that represent custom properties such as the 3D coordinates of nodes/atoms, for exmaple.

docs.title: Default Features
docs.text:
The graph representations that can be downloaded already come with a pre-defined encoding of numeric node and edge feature vectors that encode specific information about the atoms and bonds of the molecular graphs. The selection of which attributes are included here is pre-determined to be a basic selection of attributes which will be explained in detail in the following sections.

All features were calculated based on the rdkit.Mol representation of the corresponding elements.

If the default feature selection is for some reason insufficient for a given task, there is the option to define custom pre-processing classes with a custom selection of features. Custom Pre-Processing

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
You can install the latest stable version from the Python Package Index (PyPi) like this:

uv pip install chem_mat_data

Warning

The stable version of the package is not yet officially released. For the time being, please use the source installation from the github repository.

Alternatively, you can install the latest development version of the package directly from the Github repository:

uv pip install git+https://github.com/the16thpythonist/chem_mat_data

Check your installation. Installing the package should provide access to the cmdata command line interface. You can check this with the following command, which should print the current version of the chem_mat_data package:

cmdata --version

docs.title: Processing New Graphs
docs.text:
The chem_mat_data package provides a pre-processed graph format in which the individual molecules of a dataset can directly be loaded in a full graph representation with numeric node and edge feature vectors to specifically simplify the training of graph neural network (GNN) models.

Assuming one trains a GNN model on such a pre-processed dataset, one might also want to use such a model for inference to predict the target properties of new elements which weren't in the initial dataset. In such a case, the new elements will have to be processed into the same graph format to be compatible to be used as input to the trained model.

To process new graphs into the same graph format, one can use the package's MoleculeProcessing class. The process method of such a processing instance takes a molecule SMILES string representation as an input and returns the corresponding graph dict representation:

from rich.pretty import pprint
from chem_mat_data.processing import MoleculeProcessing

processing = MoleculeProcessing()

smiles: str = 'C1=CC=CC=C1CCN'
graph: dict = processing.process(smiles)
pprint(graph)

docs.title: Rejected and restricted datasets
docs.text:
Datasets that have been investigated and must not be added to ChemMatData, with the reason and the evidence behind it.

This is the complement to MISSING_DATASETS.md, which lists candidates to add. The point of both is the same: not to spend an afternoon re-deriving a conclusion someone already reached.

If you are the extraction agent: read this before stage 1. If the publication URL, the data record, or the upstream database you are about to investigate appears below, stop and tell the human, quoting the entry. Do not re-research it and do not proceed on your own judgement — the entries here were decided by a person, and only a person can change one.

A rejection is not always permanent. Each entry records what would have to change.

docs.title: tmQMg-L — ligand library of transition metal complexes
docs.text:
Publication Kneiding, H., Nova, A. & Balcells, D. Directional multiobjective optimization of metal complexes at the billion-system scale. Nat. Comput. Sci. 4, 263–273 (2024) — 10.1038/s43588-024-00616-5 Data record https://github.com/uiocompcat/tmQMg-L · Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.10374523 What it is 35,466 ligands cut out of the tmQMg complexes, with SMILES, metal-coordinating atom indices, NBO-derived formal charges and computed descriptors Decided 2026-08-13, by the maintainer Evidence rejected/tmqmg_l_charge-license-review.md

Two independent reasons, either sufficient on its own.

1. The data is CC BY-NC 4.0. The NonCommercial condition would bind every downstream ChemMatData user, not just this project. Verified rather than assumed: the LICENSE file is the unmodified CC BY-NC 4.0 legal code (MD5 fff4b145b044f5755732fda1d3aeda8c, first line Attribution-NonCommercial 4.0 International), zero occurrences of ShareAlike or NoDerivatives, and Zenodo's API independently reports cc-by-nc-4.0.

Do not read GitHub's sidebar as evidence here. The GitHub API reports this repo as "spdx_id": "NOASSERTION", "name": "Other", which looks like an unclear licence and is not one — CC BY-NC 4.0 simply is not in GitHub's licence picklist. This misled the initial briefing for the run; the LICENSE file itself is unambiguous.

2. The upstream is the Cambridge Structural Database, reached via tmQM and tmQMg. The CCDC's published position is that CSD data may not be redistributed, and its licence requires a separate signed agreement to distribute derived datasets externally. CSD refcodes appear verbatim in the redistributed files. No evidence of CCDC permission was found.

Revisit if: the CCDC grants written permission for redistribution of CSD-derived data, or the authors relicense the record under permissive terms. Neither is likely without asking.

Note: this was extracted once, on 2026-08-13, as a deliberate end-to-end test of the extraction pipeline, with the licence override approved for the test only. The dataset, its script and its 400 MB of artifacts were removed the same day. The licence review is kept because re-deriving the CCDC position took real work.

docs.title: polymer_tg — polymer glass transition temperatures
docs.text:
Publication J. Chem. Inf. Model. 61 (2021) — 10.1021/acs.jcim.1c01031 Data record The article's Supporting Information, files ci1c01031_si_002.xlsx and ci1c01031_si_003.xlsx What it is 566 polymers as repeat-unit SMILES with MD-simulated glass transition temperatures in °C Decided 2026-08-19, by the maintainer Status Script-only, never published

The article reserves rights and the one permissive branch of its SI terms does not apply. pubs.acs.org is Cloudflare-walled, which is why an earlier pass could only argue from ACS's site-wide policy. A Wayback snapshot of the article record page (2025-06-22) renders the Supporting Information block in full, and it shows: "Copyright (c) 2021 American Chemical Society", a "Request reuse permissions" link, a hard paywall ("Purchase this article for 48 hours $48.00"), and zero occurrences of "Creative Commons" anywhere on the page. The SI terms read:

"Such files may be downloaded by article for research use (if there is a public use license linked to the relevant article, that license may permit other uses). Permission may be obtained from ACS for other uses through requests via the RightsLink permission system."

That permission is conditional and the condition fails — six independent indexes agree no public-use licence is linked to this article. So what exists is permission to download for research use, which is not permission to redistribute.

A second, independent reason: the upstream is PoLyInfo (NIMS MatNavi), whose terms are registration-gated and prohibit bulk acquisition ("Web scraping of data is prohibited!").

Revisit if: ACS grants a RightsLink permission for redistribution of ci1c01031_si_002.xlsx and ci1c01031_si_003.xlsx as a downloadable dataset — note ACS's permissions page pre-declares that it does not grant permission for some redistribution classes — or the authors republish the data under an open licence elsewhere. Do not re-research the licence itself: this was settled from the authoritative record, not inferred, and no further searching will change it.

(2022) — 10.1126/sciadv.abn9545 Data record https://github.com/jsunn-y/PolymerGasMembraneML What it is 778 polymers with experimentally measured gas permeabilities (log10 Barrer) for He, H2, O2, N2, CO2 and CH4 Decided 2026-08-19, by the maintainer Status Script-only, never published

A permissive wrapper licence contradicted by its own repository, over a database that forbids bulk acquisition. The repo carries a root LICENSE file containing the MIT licence, but:

  1. The repo's own README points to a CC-BY-NC (NonCommercial) paper, contradicting that MIT file.
  2. The upstream is PoLyInfo (NIMS MatNavi) — registration-gated, bulk acquisition prohibited — together with the Membrane Society of Australasia Polymer Gas Separation Membrane Database.

This is deliberately treated differently from zinc250k, where an Apache-2.0 repository licence was accepted: there the data file sat inside the licensed repository with nothing contradicting it, and the upstream (ZINC) affirmatively permits sharing the results of a screen. Here the repository contradicts itself and the upstream prohibits the acquisition.

Revisit if: the authors clarify which licence governs the data files, or NIMS grants redistribution permission for the PoLyInfo-derived values.

No licence exists, and the vendor's terms affirmatively forbid the redistribution. This is the most thoroughly established negative in the licence review. Checked, over a decade of snapshots: the current and June-2021 Terms of Use (byte-identical), the database download page across 8 Wayback snapshots spanning 2015–2025, /legal (404), /privacy, the entire doc.mcule.com wiki, FAIRsharing and re3data. Zero licence, copyright or reuse statements anywhere. Mcule's Terms of Use then go further and prohibit what redistribution here would require.

This is a commercial vendor's price list — the compound prices are the product Mcule sells. It is categorically unlike the research datasets elsewhere in this collection.

Revisit if: Mcule grants written permission to redistribute a sample of the purchasable collection with prices. Nothing short of that changes the answer — do not re-research the licence, it was settled from the vendor's own terms across a decade of captures.

docs.title: tadf — TADF/OLED virtual screening molecules
docs.text:
Publication Gómez-Bombarelli, R. et al. Design of efficient molecular organic light-emitting diodes by a high-throughput virtual screening and experimental approach. Nat. Mater. 15, 1120–1127 (2016) — 10.1038/nmat4717 Data record None exists. The file used was source/tadf.csv on a KIT group file share What it is 460,199 organic molecules from a high-throughput virtual screen for thermally activated delayed fluorescence OLED emitters Decided 2026-08-19, by the maintainer Status Was published (460,199 compounds); removed from metadata.yml and the script now refuses to run. The files were left on the remote share.

This is a provenance and consent failure, not a publisher-copyright one. An earlier pass blocked it on the Springer "all rights reserved" notice; that reasoning was wrong and has been corrected, though the conclusion stands.

1. The Springer SI notice does not govern this data. The article's SI PDF contains roughly 300 structures (46 lead candidates, ~168 fragments, ~88 calibration compounds) — not 460,199. Decisively: all 46 SI lead-candidate SMILES were canonicalised and matched 46/46 against tadf.csv, and our file holds the full-precision values the SI only prints rounded — SI 0.121 / 0.061 / 2.94 / 0.07 against our 0.121228915 / 0.06096116 / 2.936687531 / 0.065375355. The SI is therefore a hand-rounded 0.01% extract of this file, not its source. Springer Nature also affirmatively disclaims intellectual property in "datasets connected to published papers", so the publisher is not a plausible rights-holder here at all.

2. But nobody who might hold rights has granted anything. An exhaustive first-hand sweep — Zenodo, Figshare, Dataverse, OSF, GitHub, Hugging Face, Kaggle, DataCite under both corresponding-author names, PubChem, and the Matter Lab's own open-data page — found no open release of this data anywhere, ten years on. The nearest neighbours are all different data: the Clean Energy Project (Figshare 9640427, CC BY 4.0) is a photovoltaic screen with a different schema; Tartarus' gdb13.csv carries license: null; and the-matter-lab/Artificial-Design-of-Organic-Emitters claims Apache-2.0 in its README with no LICENSE file and is a different molecule set regardless.

3. The authors' own most recent word on this exact dataset is access-gated. Friederich, Krenn, Tamblyn & Aspuru-Guzik, Mach. Learn.: Sci. Technol. 2, 025027 (2021) — itself published CC-BY-4.0, so these authors plainly know how to signal openness when they intend it — states the data is "available upon reasonable request from the authors". That is the opposite of an open release.

4. Samsung co-authorship clouds who could even grant it. The original screen was a joint academic–industrial project with Samsung SAIT / Samsung Research America co-authors, so a willing academic author may lack unilateral authority to release it.

5. The copy reached this project informally. Researcher-to-researcher, with no documented grant of redistribution rights.

An open legal question is deliberately left open. Springer's site-terms restriction is contractual rather than copyright-based, which raises but does not settle whether a computed SMILES + TD-DFT property table is "facts" below the originality threshold (Feist) in the first place. Given the Ilm-NMR-P31 precedent in this same file — where EU sui generis database-right terms were taken seriously rather than assumed away — and ChemMatData's German context, that is a maintainer-level legal call, not one to settle in passing.

Revisit if: the provenance can be established internally. The obvious lead is to ask Pascal Friederich (AiMat, KIT) how source/tadf.csv came to be on the group's bwSyncAndShare share, where it has sat since visual_graph_datasets' first release — he was a postdoc in the Aspuru-Guzik group, which is the natural explanation for a 460k-row file that exists nowhere public. If the answer is that the authors provided it, that is provenance no amount of web searching can recover, and the dataset may be revivable on that basis together with a permission from the authors. Failing that, a Springer Nature permission request would be needed.

docs.title: Ilm-NMR-P31 — ³¹P NMR chemical shifts
docs.text:
Publication 10.1186/s13321-023-00792-y Data record https://zenodo.org/records/20762603 — record licence CC BY 4.0 Decided 2026-08-12, by the maintainer Evidence dataset_redistribution_analysis.md

The record's own licence is clean; the problem is upstream, and it splits the dataset in two:

Source block Structures Position HBP — Tebby, Handbook of ³¹P NMR Data, CRC Press, 1991 6,608 Sui generis term expired 31 Dec 2012 (§137g(2) UrhG); US maker, likely outside Art. 11. Usable. Lan1/2/3 — Landolt-Börnstein III/40H, Springer, 2013/14 5,114 Term runs to ~2029; German maker. Not usable.

Decision: the middle path — only the HBP-derived block may be used. The Landolt-Börnstein-derived structures are held back until the database right expires (~2029), unless Springer grants permission first.

Second, independent reason not to publish this dataset at all as it stands: 196 of its geometries are a chemically different species from their own published formula — gas-phase optimisation let ion pairs react and waters of hydration dissociate, with one "bond" measuring 7.6 Å. That is a data-quality decision that has not been made, separate from the licence one.

docs.title: ChEMBL and ShareAlike
docs.text:
Decided 2026-08-19 by the maintainer. ChEMBL is CC BY-SA 3.0 — attribution and ShareAlike. The project complies: ChEMBL-derived datasets are attributed to ChEMBL and labelled CC-BY-SA-3.0 in their metadata, so the reciprocal obligation is passed on to whoever downloads them.

Applies to twelve datasets: dud_e, riniker_1, riniker_1_filtered, riniker_2, bl_chembl_reg, bl_chembl_cls, lipophilicity, dpp4, moleculeace, pparg_binding, esnuel_mca, esnuel_maa.

  • Evidence and the options that were weighed: chembl_licensing_analysis.md
  • The field, its shape, and what it commits the project to: ADR 009

If you are the extraction agent and your dataset is ChEMBL-derived: this no longer needs escalating on the ChEMBL ground alone. Record CC-BY-SA-3.0 in the licence stage with ChEMBL named as upstream_database, put the same identifier in the metadata draft's license field, and note that the gate will still escalate ShareAlike — that is expected, and the human override should cite this entry. Any other licence problem with your dataset is still yours to escalate on its own merits.

Still worth doing, and would only relax this: asking EMBL-EBI whether ShareAlike legally attaches to a filtered, re-encoded dataset of computed properties. Option A was taken as the conservative answer without that confirmation.

docs.title: Adding an entry
docs.text:
Record enough that nobody has to redo the research:

  • Every identifier the dataset can be reached by — publication DOI, record URL, mirrors. An agent arriving from a different link must still find the entry.
  • What was actually verified, not what was concluded. File hashes, quoted licence text, the URL of the terms. A conclusion with no evidence gets re-derived anyway.
  • Who decided and when. These are human decisions; an agent may not add or remove one.
  • What would have to change for the answer to be different.

If the reasoning is long, put it in docs/rejected/ and link it, as with the tmQMg-L licence review.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The chem_mat_data package mainly aims to provide a Python and command line API which can be used to easily download and access chemistry and material science datasets for machine learning with a specific focus on graph neural networks. One core question in the design of this package is in which format to provide these datasets to the end user. This is a tricky matter because the datasets may have slightly different formats themselves and might even have slighlty different objectives. For example, there can be a distinction between node-level and graph-level tasks which changes the way in which the ground truth labels have to be provided. Another difference could be that some datasets may consists of different molecules while other datasets consist of the same molecule over and over again, only with different geometries.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: The decision made for this package is to provide datasets in two formats simultaneously: - raw. This format should be as close as possible to the original domain-specific representation that the dataset is provided in. For most datasets this will likely be a CSV file containing the SMILES codes of different molecules associated with ground truth classification and regression labels. Additionally, this raw representation could be extended with additional information about the geometric configurations. - processed. In addition to the raw format, each dataset should also be provided in the already processed format. In this format, the individual elements of the dataset are already present as abstract graph structures consisting of nodes (atoms) connected by edges (bonds). Additionally each node and edge should be associated with a numeric feature vector which has been extracted using the Cheminformatics library RDKit.

docs.title: Advantages
docs.text:
Ease of use. The main advantage of providing the processed version of the dataset directly is that this makes it immensly easy to use the dataset to train a graph neural network. The graph format used in the package is a generic one and the package specifically aims to provide adapters that transform these generic graph structures into the necessary object instances required for the most common graph learning libraries such as pytorch geometric and jraph. This ultimately means that a dataset is training-ready in a couple lines of code.

Standardization. The processed graph structures already contain numeric feature vectors for the nodes and edges which have been obtained from RDKit. If everyone were to use the same processing / featurization pipeline, this would lead to more comparable results in the end.

docs.title: Disadvantages
docs.text:
Dataset size. A main disadvantage of the processed datasets is the significantly increased size required to encode the full graph structure which will affect the download speed and the storage requirements especially for larger datasets.

Rigidity. The processed graph structures already contain numeric feature vectors for the nodes and edges which have been obtained from RDKit. Besides a standardization effect, this also means that. However, the package also provides the means to implement custom processing on top of the raw dataset representations if desired.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: implemented

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
The package also provides the various datasets to be downloaded in a processed format where the various molecules are in a generic graph representation. The question that arises in this situation is how to structure this graph representation, especially since different datasets may have different requirements.

The main requirements for this graph representation are: - support for rich metadata at each level of the graph: node-, edge- and graph-level - support for graph-level feature and label annotations - support for node-level feature vectors - support for edge-level feature vectors

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
The decision is to use a custom graph representation specifically created by and for this package called a GraphDict representation. This represents a graph as a simple python native dictionary structure where special keys identify the various parts of the graph representation. The most important keys are the following:

  • node_indices: The integer indices of the nodes
  • node_attributes: A node feature vector for each node in the same order as the node indices
  • edge_indices: a list of node index tuples which define which nodes are connected by edges
  • edge_attributes: A edge feature vector for each edge in the same order as the edge indices
  • graph_labels: A list of label annotations for the graph as a whole

Besides these main keys, the primary feature of the graph dict representation is that it is supposed to be flexible and that additional properties can be added dynamically by using one of the special prefixes node_, edge_ and graph_ to indicate at which level of the graph to attach the information to.

docs.title: Advantages
docs.text:
Native. The major advantage of this graph representation is that it only relies on python native datastructures such as dictionaries and lists and by extension is therefore also easily JSON encodable. Being able to JSON encode is very important for the transfer of the datasets over the internet and also the potential compatibility with other programming languages when compared to a pickle dump for example.

Generic and Flexible. The flexible format allows to add additional information for datasets that need it without having to over-complicate the core data structure.

docs.title: Disadvantages
docs.text: Custom Format. It is a custom format that most people will not be initially familiar with. This is in contrast to using more common formats such as networkx Graph instances for example, which some people might already have familarity with. However, we argue that the format is simple enough to understand and also simple enough to convert to a more common format such as networkx - especially if the necessary adapaters are provided as part of the package as well.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
The ChemMatData package provides the possibility to download graph datasets from a remote file share server. These datasets can either be in the "raw" format - in the case of purely molecular datasets this usually means a CSV file with the molecule SMILES representations annotated with the target values. But more importantly, these datasets can be downloaded in the already pre-processed format and easily loaded into the popular graph deep learning libraries.

There exists a command line interface and a programming interface to very easily load a dataset with a single function call. The problem now is that repeated calls to this function would download the dataset anew each time. This would require a constant internet connection and could take a significant amount of time for larger datasets.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
The mitigate the recurring runtime of re-downloading the datasets each time, a local caching mechanism was added which was inspired by package managers such as pip which also maintain a similar caching mechanism. Whenever a dataset is downloaded, the downloaded files will be placed into a user-specific caching folder. For all subsequent retrievals of the dataset, the cached version will be used instead.

Inside the cache, each dataset is enumerated by its unique string name and the dataset type (raw or processed).

docs.title: Advantages
docs.text: Runtime. The clear advantage of a local cache is the runtime. Especially for large datasert and/or repeated execution of the dataset loading functionality, a local cahce will result in a clear reduction in runtime and bandwith.

docs.title: Disadvantages
docs.text:
User Storage. For the user, the cache will eat up some storage capacity, which may or may not be significant depending on the number and size of the stored datasets. Although, this likely won't be a problem as the archived versions of even the largest datasets currently do now exceed a GB in size.

Management Overhead. On the development side, the cache introduces another layer of complexity. Before fetching the datasets, we need to check if the dataset exists in the cache and after downloading the dataset we need to add the dataset to the cache.

docs.text: implemented

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
The ChemMatData package provides molecular datasets for machine learning applications, particularly for training graph neural networks. As datasets grow larger (100k+ molecules), several challenges emerge:

Memory Constraints: Loading entire datasets into memory becomes problematic. A single molecular graph with features can require several kilobytes, meaning a 100k molecule dataset can easily consume multiple gigabytes of RAM. This limits the ability to work with large datasets on consumer hardware or to train multiple models concurrently on shared infrastructure.

Processing Bottlenecks: Converting molecular representations (SMILES strings or XYZ structures) to graph representations using RDKit is CPU-intensive (~0.5ms per molecule). For large datasets, processing all molecules upfront creates a significant startup delay before training can begin. Additionally, if users want to experiment with different featurization approaches, reprocessing the entire dataset each time is inefficient.

Training Requirements: Modern deep learning frameworks (PyTorch, JAX) use data loaders that iterate through datasets multiple times during training. These frameworks are designed to work efficiently with streaming data, loading and processing batches on-demand rather than requiring the entire dataset in memory.

Multiple Data Formats: Molecular datasets come in different formats: - SMILES strings represent 2D connectivity (compact, text-based) - XYZ files include 3D atomic coordinates (essential for conformer-dependent properties)

Supporting both formats while maintaining a unified API is important for flexibility across different modeling tasks.

Use Case Flexibility: Different use cases have different requirements: - Quick prototyping benefits from fast iteration with small subsets - Large-scale experiments need to handle datasets that exceed available RAM - Custom featurization pipelines require processing flexibility without re-downloading datasets - 3D property prediction requires access to geometric information from XYZ datasets

The existing approach of providing pre-processed datasets (ADR 001) works well for convenience but doesn't address these scalability challenges for large datasets, custom processing needs, or flexible format support.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Implement a streaming dataset architecture with four main classes in chem_mat_data/dataset.py:

docs.title: 1. SmilesDataset
docs.text: A lazy-loading dataset that streams SMILES strings and properties from CSV files line-by-line using Python's csv.DictReader. Only one row is loaded into memory at a time, providing minimal memory footprint. Used for 2D molecular datasets where only connectivity matters.

docs.title: 2. XyzDataset
docs.text: A lazy-loading dataset that streams 3D molecular structures from XYZ file bundles. Iterates through individual .xyz files (one per molecule) stored in an xyz_bundle folder, yielding atomic coordinates, atomic numbers, and properties. Supports multiple XYZ format parsers (default, qm9, hopv15) to handle different XYZ file specifications. Essential for tasks requiring 3D geometric information.

docs.title: 3. GraphDataset
docs.text:
Extends the streaming approach to convert raw molecular representations (from either SmilesDataset or XyzDataset) into graph dict representations on-the-fly. Automatically detects which dataset type to use based on what's available (tries .csv first, then .xyz_bundle). Supports two processing modes:

Sequential Mode (num_workers=0): - True streaming: processes one molecule at a time - Minimal memory usage - Single-threaded processing (~2000 mol/s for typical molecules) - Best for memory-constrained environments or simple molecules

Parallel Mode (num_workers>0): - Multi-process architecture for CPU-bound parallelism - Producer thread reads raw data (SMILES/XYZ) and distributes work to worker processes - Worker processes convert raw data to Mol objects then to graphs in parallel (bypasses Python GIL) - Collector thread reorders results to maintain dataset order - Results buffer allows main iterator to suspend at yield without deadlock - Better throughput for complex molecules or CPU-intensive custom processing

Auto-Detection Architecture: - Uses try-except approach: attempts SmilesDataset first, falls back to XyzDataset - Stores dataset_type string ('smiles' or 'xyz') for worker initialization - Workers receive raw data (SMILES strings or XYZ dicts) and convert in parallel - Transparent to users - same API regardless of underlying format

docs.title: 4. ShuffleDataset
docs.text: Wrapper that provides approximate shuffling using a fixed-size shuffle buffer. This enables training with shuffled data without loading the entire dataset into memory. The buffer size controls the trade-off between shuffling quality and memory usage.

docs.title: Architecture Highlights
docs.text:
Deadlock Prevention: The parallel mode uses a sophisticated producer-collector thread architecture where a separate collector thread continuously drains the result queue. This prevents deadlock when the main iterator suspends at yield, ensuring worker processes never block on a full queue.

Order Preservation: Workers may complete molecules out of order (due to varying complexity), but the collector thread uses a priority queue (heap) to reorder results before yielding them, maintaining the original dataset sequence.

Queue Design: - Input queue: bounded (provides backpressure) - Result queue: unbounded (critical for deadlock prevention) - Results buffer: thread-local queue (low overhead, no pickling)

Integration: Datasets work seamlessly with the existing ensure_dataset() function, automatically downloading and caching raw CSV files when needed.

docs.title: Advantages
docs.text:
Memory Efficiency: Streaming enables working with arbitrarily large datasets on limited hardware. Only the data currently being processed needs to be in memory, not the entire dataset. This is particularly important for cloud environments where memory is a cost factor.

Multiple Format Support: Unified API for both SMILES-based and XYZ-based datasets enables seamless handling of 2D connectivity and 3D geometric information. Auto-detection makes format handling transparent to users.

Flexible Processing: Users can apply custom featurization by subclassing MoleculeProcessing and providing it to GraphDataset. The streaming approach means custom processing happens on-demand rather than requiring reprocessing of stored datasets. Works identically for both SMILES and XYZ sources.

Faster Startup: Training can begin immediately as data is streamed and processed on-the-fly, rather than waiting for the entire dataset to be loaded and processed upfront.

True Parallelism: Multi-process architecture bypasses Python's GIL, enabling true CPU parallelism for graph processing. This scales effectively with CPU cores for complex molecules or custom processing. Raw data format (SMILES strings or XYZ dicts) minimizes pickling overhead.

Composability: The wrapper pattern (ShuffleDataset) allows building more complex data pipelines by composing simple components, similar to PyTorch's dataset philosophy.

API Consistency: Streaming datasets implement the standard Python iterator protocol (__iter__ and __len__), making them compatible with existing code that expects iterable datasets. Same interface regardless of underlying format.

docs.title: Disadvantages
docs.text:
Complexity: The parallel processing implementation is significantly more complex than simple in-memory loading, particularly the deadlock prevention architecture with multiple threads and processes. Supporting multiple dataset formats (SMILES and XYZ) adds additional complexity with the auto-detection mechanism. This increases maintenance burden and makes debugging more challenging.

Parallel Overhead: For simple molecules, parallel processing is actually slower than sequential due to overhead (~0.6ms per molecule for pickling, queue operations, and thread coordination vs ~0.5ms processing time). The complexity of the parallel code only pays off for complex molecules or CPU-intensive custom processing.

No Random Access: Streaming datasets don't support index-based access (e.g., dataset[42]). This is incompatible with some training frameworks or use cases that require random access patterns. However, this is mitigated by the ShuffleDataset wrapper for common training scenarios.

Repeated Iteration Overhead: Each iteration through the dataset requires re-reading the raw data (CSV or XYZ files) and re-processing molecules. For training that requires multiple epochs, this processing cost is paid repeatedly. In contrast, pre-processed datasets only pay the cost once during download.

Format-Specific Parameters: XyzDataset requires additional parameters (parser_cls) that aren't needed for SmilesDataset. This creates some API inconsistency, though GraphDataset handles this through auto-detection and parameter forwarding.

Less Discoverable: Users familiar with the pre-processed datasets (ADR 001) may not immediately discover the streaming alternative. Documentation and examples are critical to guide users toward the appropriate solution for their use case, including when to use SMILES vs XYZ formats.

Processing Variance: Unlike pre-processed datasets where all users get identical featurization, streaming datasets with custom processing classes can lead to less comparable results across different experiments or research groups.

Currently, there are two major bottlenecks in the extension of the ChemMatDatabase: 1. The discovery of new datasets in the scientific literature 2. The processing of the very different file formats into a unified format

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
The chem_mat_data package was originally designed exclusively for small organic molecules, using MoleculeProcessing to convert SMILES strings into graph representations via RDKit. Reviewer feedback on the associated HDF (Hyperdimensional Fingerprints) paper requested evaluation on broader compound classes, particularly organometallics and transition metal complexes (TMCs).

TMCs present fundamental challenges that the existing organic pipeline cannot handle:

  • RDKit sanitization failures. RDKit enforces valence rules designed for organic chemistry. Transition metals routinely violate these rules (e.g., Fe with 6 coordinate bonds), causing MolFromSmiles to return None for 5-70% of TMC SMILES depending on the dataset.
  • Dative bonds. The dominant bond type in coordination chemistry (ligand donates an electron pair to the metal) is not in the organic bond type vocabulary (single, double, triple, aromatic).
  • Haptic bonding. Metallocenes and arene complexes involve multi-center bonding where a metal interacts with an entire ring's pi system, which cannot be faithfully represented as atom-pair bonds.
  • Element coverage. The organic atom one-hot encoding covers only 19 elements. TMC datasets involve all 30 transition metals (Sc-Zn, Y-Cd, Hf-Hg).
  • Metal-specific properties. d-electron count, oxidation state, coordination geometry, and spin state are critical for predicting TMC properties but have no analogue in organic chemistry.

docs.title: Decomposed Raw Format
docs.text:
Instead of representing a TMC as a single whole-complex SMILES (which is fragile and lossy), the raw format uses a decomposed representation: a metal element symbol, a list of individual ligand SMILES strings, and connecting atom indices specifying which ligand atoms coordinate to the metal. This mirrors how the most successful TMC ML methods work (ELECTRUM, RACs, molSimplify) and keeps ligand SMILES fully organic and RDKit-compatible.

A dedicated load_tmc_dataset() function handles loading this richer tabular format, separate from the organic load_smiles_dataset().

docs.title: Sibling Processing Class
docs.text:
A new MetalOrganicProcessing class was created as a sibling to MoleculeProcessing (both conceptually inherit from AbstractProcessing) rather than a subclass. The organic assumptions in MoleculeProcessing (single SMILES input, organic element vocabulary, no dative bonds, Crippen logP) are too deeply embedded to override cleanly. The sibling approach avoids fighting inherited behavior while reusing the same encoder infrastructure (OneHotEncoder, chem_prop, EncoderBase).

The process() method takes the decomposed input and assembles a unified molecular graph by:

  1. Creating the metal center as node 0 with TMC-specific features.
  2. Parsing each ligand SMILES separately (with lenient sanitization that skips valence checks).
  3. Adding intra-ligand bonds as standard edges.
  4. Adding dative bond edges from each ligand's donor atoms to the metal node.

docs.title: Feature Encoding (91 / 18 / 5 dimensions)
docs.text:
Node features (91 dims): 51-element one-hot (20 common organic + 30 TMs + unknown), hybridization (10 dims, including SP3D2), total degree (13 dims, covering CN 0-12), hydrogen count, atomic mass, formal charge, aromaticity, ring membership, plus TMC-specific continuous features: is_metal_center flag, Pauling electronegativity, covalent radius, van der Waals radius, periodic table period and group, d-electron count, and outer electron count. Electronegativity and group number use bundled Python dictionary lookup tables (~50 entries each).

Edge features (18 dims): Bond type one-hot (7 dims, adding DATIVE and ZERO to the organic types), stereo, aromaticity, ring membership, conjugation, bond order as continuous value, plus three manually computed TMC features: is_dative flag, dative_direction (+1 for donor-to-metal, -1 for reverse, 0 for non-dative), and is_metal_metal flag for future polynuclear support.

Graph features (5 dims): Molecular weight, total charge, number of metal centers (always 1 for now), coordination number, and metal atomic number.

docs.title: Haptic Bonding Strategy
docs.text: The star pattern (Strategy A) is used as the default: each atom in a haptic ligand (e.g., each of the 5 carbons in a cyclopentadienyl ring) gets an individual edge to the metal. This over-counts the coordination number but is compatible with all standard GNN architectures (GCN, GAT, GIN, MPNN). The is_haptic edge feature is available in the full encoding scheme (when metadata is provided) to let models distinguish haptic from sigma/dative bonds.

docs.title: Scope: Mononuclear Only
docs.text: The initial implementation targets mononuclear complexes (single metal center), which covers the primary benchmark datasets (tmQMg, ELECTRUM coordination number and oxidation state datasets). Graph-level features like coordination number and metal atomic number assume a single metal. Polynuclear support (metal-metal bonds, bridging ligands) is designed for but not yet implemented.

docs.title: Advantages
docs.text:
High compatibility. By decomposing TMCs into organic ligand fragments, the entire RDKit ecosystem works for ligand processing without workarounds. Lenient sanitization (skipping valence checks) handles the remaining edge cases where ligand fragments have metal-influenced valences.

Clean separation. Organic and TMC processing pipelines do not interfere with each other. Users working only with organic molecules are completely unaffected. TMC users get purpose-built features validated against the ELECTRUM, RACs, and tmQMg benchmarks.

Extensibility. The decomposed format and sibling class pattern make it straightforward to add support for new compound classes (MOFs, polymers) as additional processing classes in the future.

docs.title: Disadvantages
docs.text:
Different feature dimensions. TMC graph datasets (91-dim nodes) and organic graph datasets (44-dim nodes) cannot be mixed in the same model without a compatibility layer. This is an inherent consequence of the different chemical information being encoded.

Heuristic donor atom detection. When connecting atom indices are not provided in the source data (as with the tmQMg dataset), donor atoms must be inferred heuristically. The current heuristic (prefer negatively charged atoms, then heteroatoms with lone pairs, then fall back to index 0) works well for classical coordination compounds but may be wrong for carbon-donor ligands like NHC carbenes.

No whole-complex graph. The decomposed representation loses inter-ligand interactions (steric clashes, hydrogen bonding between ligands, trans influence) that require knowing the full 3D arrangement. For tasks where these matter, 3D coordinates would need to be incorporated as an additional input.

docs.title: Dataset Category and Version Compatibility Metadata
Status
docs.text: implemented

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
With the introduction of transition metal complex (TMC) support (see ADR 006), the package now hosts datasets that are fundamentally different from the original organic molecule datasets: different feature dimensions (91 vs 44 node dims), different raw column schemas (decomposed metal + ligand SMILES vs single SMILES column), different processing classes (MetalOrganicProcessing vs MoleculeProcessing), and different loader functions (load_tmc_dataset vs load_smiles_dataset).

Two problems arise:

  1. Delineation. There is no way for a user (or the system) to know whether a dataset in the registry is an organic molecule dataset or a TMC dataset. A user calling load_smiles_dataset('tmqmg') would get a DataFrame with unexpected columns (metal, ligand_smiles instead of smiles). The CLI cmdata list shows all datasets in a flat list with no indication of their type.

  2. Version compatibility. TMC datasets require MetalOrganicProcessing which was introduced in version 1.7.0. A user on version 1.6.0 who sees a TMC dataset in cmdata list and tries to download and load it would get confusing errors. Similarly, XYZ-format datasets require the XYZ parsing support introduced in version 1.1.0.

docs.title: Category Field
docs.text:
A category string field was added to the per-dataset metadata in metadata.yml. The field is optional — datasets that lack it default to "organic" throughout the system. Currently defined categories:

  • "organic" — standard small molecule datasets loaded via load_smiles_dataset() / load_graph_dataset()
  • "tmc" — transition metal complex datasets loaded via load_tmc_dataset() / load_graph_dataset()

The category is displayed in both the CLI dataset list (as a dedicated column) and the dataset detail view. The load_tmc_dataset() function performs a soft validation check: if the dataset metadata has a category other than "tmc", it logs a warning suggesting the user may want load_smiles_dataset() instead. This is advisory only — the load proceeds regardless.

The documentation generation command (cmmanage docs collect-datasets) also includes the category column in the generated dataset table.

docs.title: Minimum Version Field
docs.text:
A min_version string field was added to the per-dataset metadata. The field is optional — datasets that lack it are treated as compatible with all versions. The value is a semantic version string (e.g., "1.7.0").

Version comparison uses packaging.version.Version (a transitive dependency already available via pip/setuptools) via the new check_version_compatible(min_version) utility function in utils.py, which compares against the installed version from the VERSION file.

The compatibility check is integrated at three levels:

  • CLI list (cmdata list). Incompatible datasets are shown with dimmed text and a (requires >=X.Y.Z) marker appended to the name. They are still visible — not hidden — so users know what is available after upgrading.
  • CLI detail (cmdata info). The min_version is displayed in the metadata table, colored green if compatible or red with the installed version if not.
  • Python loaders. load_smiles_dataset(), load_graph_dataset(), and load_tmc_dataset() each attempt a lightweight metadata fetch and log a logging.warning if the installed version is below the requirement. The warning is non-blocking — loading proceeds regardless, since the dataset might still work partially with an older version.

All checks are wrapped in try/except so they never prevent loading even if metadata is unavailable (e.g., for local-only datasets or when the file share is unreachable).

docs.title: Version Assignments
docs.text:
• Existing organic CSV datasets: No min_version field (always compatible).
  • XYZ-format datasets (e.g., _test2): min_version: "1.1.0" (when XYZ support was introduced).
  • TMC datasets (e.g., tmqmg): min_version: "1.7.0" (when MetalOrganicProcessing is introduced).

New dataset processing scripts should include min_version in their METADATA dict so it is automatically written to the generated metadata.yml.

docs.title: Advantages
docs.text:
Backwards compatible. Both fields are optional with sensible defaults ("organic" for category, always-compatible for min_version). Existing metadata files, experiment archives, and API calls work without modification. The system gracefully handles datasets from before these fields existed.

User-friendly. Instead of cryptic import errors or shape mismatches, users get clear signals: the CLI shows which datasets need a newer version, and the loaders warn when category or version don't match.

Extensible. New categories (e.g., "mof", "polymer") and new version requirements can be added to future datasets without any code changes — only metadata entries.

docs.title: Disadvantages
docs.text:
Metadata fetch overhead. The version check in Python loaders requires fetching metadata before loading the actual dataset. This adds a small overhead (typically a local cache hit). The check is wrapped in try/except so it never blocks, but it does add latency on the first call when metadata must be downloaded from the file share.

Soft enforcement only. Both the category and version checks are warnings, not errors. A determined user can still load a TMC dataset with load_smiles_dataset() or load a dataset requiring 1.7.0 on version 1.6.0. This is a deliberate trade-off: hard errors would be more disruptive than the problems they prevent, and there are legitimate cases where partial loading is useful (e.g., inspecting raw CSV columns).

docs.title: Status
docs.text: implemented

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
The ChemMatData package provides a growing catalog of chemistry and materials-science datasets for graph neural network research. Two bottlenecks limit the expansion of this catalog (see also ADR 005):

  1. Finding new datasets in the scientific literature.
  2. Processing each dataset's raw files into the unified graph format.

ADR 005 addresses the second bottleneck with the cmmanage agent workflow: given a publication URL, an LLM agent reads the paper, downloads the data, and generates a processing script. That workflow is effective but expensive — each invocation browses a paper, visits repository links, and runs multiple LLM reasoning steps. At the scale of the full OpenAlex index (hundreds of millions of works, tens of thousands new per week in chemistry and materials science alone), running the agent on every paper is neither practical nor economical.

What is needed is a cheap upstream filter that can scan the literature at scale and produce a short list of papers likely to publish a reusable dataset. Only those flagged papers are then worth feeding to the expensive agent pipeline for final verification.

The upstream Dataset-Discovery-Pipeline repository provides exactly this filter: it walks the OpenAlex API for chemistry and materials-science papers and applies a fine-tuned TinyLlama-1.1B sequence classifier to the title and abstract of each work, flagging those whose language suggests a dataset release. The classifier is a QLoRA adapter (~13 MB) over the TinyLlama/TinyLlama-1.1B-Chat-v1.0 base model and was trained on a manually labeled corpus of ~2,000 papers.

The question is how to integrate this filter into ChemMatData as a composable, offline-capable CLI tool that fits the existing cmmanage architecture.

docs.title: Two-Stage Filter Architecture
docs.text:
The discovery pipeline is positioned as a cheap upstream filter that feeds into the expensive downstream agent (ADR 005). The pipeline intentionally over-includes (default threshold 0.05, tuned for recall over precision on the upstream test set) because missing a genuine dataset release is more costly than sending a few false positives to the agent step, which can reject them quickly.

The boundary between the two stages is a simple file: the discovery pipeline outputs a list of flagged OpenAlex IDs and DOI URLs, and the agent's identify command takes a URL as input. No shared state, no API coupling — just a file hand-off.

docs.title: CLI Surface: Three Command Shapes
docs.text:
The pipeline is exposed under cmmanage discover with five commands organized around two usage patterns:

Two-step pattern (fetch → score): Separates data acquisition from classification. fetch writes a JSONL file of raw records; score reads that JSONL file, loads the classifier, and writes both an _all and a _flagged output. This is useful when the user wants to inspect the fetched data before scoring, re-score with a different threshold without re-fetching, or run the two steps on different machines (e.g., fetch on a server with network access, score on a GPU node).

Single-pass pattern (stream): Interleaves fetching and classification in one command, writing scored results to a CSV as they come in with live terminal progress. This is the convenient default for most users who just want to run the pipeline end-to-end. The CSV columns (openalex_id, url, score, flagged, publication_year) are designed to be directly openable in a spreadsheet for manual review.

Utility commands (model-info, model-download): Diagnostic and setup helpers. model-info is read-only — it shows the cache location and dependency status without touching the filesystem. model-download pre-fetches the adapter archive, useful for offline environments or CI warmup.

All three fetch-capable commands (fetch, score, stream) share the same classifier options (--device, --no-quantize, --max-length, --model-url) so users can switch between the two-step and single-pass workflows without learning different flags.

docs.title: Flat Sidecar Files for Resumable State
docs.text:
Pagination and de-duplication state is stored in two plain-text sidecar files next to the output:

  • <output>.cursor — a single-line file containing the OpenAlex next_cursor token.
  • <output>.ids — a newline-delimited set of OpenAlex IDs already written to the output.

This design was chosen over SQLite, JSON, or an in-memory-only approach for several reasons:

  • Inspectable. A user can cat or wc -l the files to understand exactly where a run stopped and how many records were processed. When a run goes wrong, the state can be edited by hand (e.g., deleting the cursor file to restart pagination while keeping the seen-ID set).
  • Atomic. The cursor file is rewritten after every batch; the IDs file is append-only with an immediate flush() after each entry. If the process is killed mid-batch, the worst case is re-fetching a single page — no corruption, no write-ahead log, no recovery procedure.
  • No dependencies. No SQLite driver, no schema migrations, no connection management. The files are just strings.

The FetchState class encapsulates this logic and supports both one-shot usage (load + update_cursor) and streaming usage as a context manager with mark_seen flushing to disk immediately.

docs.title: Model Distribution via Nextcloud
docs.text:
The classifier adapter is distributed as a tar.gz archive hosted on the same Nextcloud instance that serves the dataset files. The URL is configured under [discovery] classifier_url in the config file, following the same pattern as the dataset file share URL.

This was chosen over HuggingFace Hub hosting because:

  • The existing Nextcloud infrastructure is already in place and trusted by the team.
  • The adapter is a single static artifact (~13 MB) that changes rarely — it does not benefit from Hub features like model cards, versioning, or community contributions.
  • Downloading from Nextcloud requires no authentication and no HuggingFace account.

The base model (TinyLlama-1.1B-Chat) is still fetched from HuggingFace Hub on first load, since it is a public model maintained by the TinyLlama team and benefits from Hub caching. The ensure_classifier_model function downloads the archive to a .tar.gz.part temporary file and renames it atomically on success, so a failed download never leaves a corrupt cache.

docs.title: TinyLlama-1.1B as the Classifier Backbone
docs.text:
The upstream pipeline chose TinyLlama-1.1B-Chat-v1.0 as the classifier backbone for a specific set of trade-offs:

  • Small enough for CPU inference. At 1.1B parameters the model runs on a laptop CPU in ~1-2 seconds per paper, which is acceptable for batch sizes of hundreds to low thousands. This makes the pipeline accessible without a GPU.
  • Large enough for language understanding. The classifier needs to distinguish dataset-release language ("we release a benchmark of 50,000 molecules") from dataset-usage language ("we evaluate on the QM9 benchmark"). A bag-of-words or TF-IDF classifier struggles with this distinction; a language model handles it well.
  • QLoRA adapter. The fine-tuned weights are a ~13 MB LoRA adapter, not a full model copy. This keeps the download small and the memory overhead low. On CUDA with bitsandbytes, 4-bit quantization further reduces memory to ~1 GB.

The threshold of 0.05 (positive-class probability) is deliberately low. At this threshold the upstream test set achieved the best F1 score, trading many false positives for very few false negatives. This is the right trade-off for a filter whose output feeds into a more expensive verification step.

docs.title: CPU-First with Optional Quantization
docs.text:
The classifier loading logic follows a capability-detection pattern:

  1. If CUDA is available and bitsandbytes is installed, load with 4-bit NF4 quantization.
  2. If CUDA is available but bitsandbytes is not, load in float16.
  3. Otherwise, load on CPU in float32.

The user can force a specific device with --device or disable quantization with --no-quantize. This layered approach ensures the pipeline works everywhere — from a CI runner with no GPU to a workstation with an A100 — without requiring the user to understand quantization configuration.

docs.title: ML Dependencies in Dev Extras
docs.text:
The ML stack (torch, transformers, peft, safetensors, accelerate, and optionally bitsandbytes) is placed in the [dev] extras group rather than the core dependencies. This keeps the base pip install chem_mat_database lightweight for users who only need the dataset loading and graph processing functionality.

A runtime check (is_ml_stack_available()) gates the classifier commands: if the ML dependencies are missing, the commands print a clear error message pointing to pip install chem_mat_database[dev] rather than crashing with an obscure import error. The model-info command always works regardless of ML availability, since its purpose is precisely to diagnose what is and isn't installed.

docs.title: Noise Suppression
docs.text:
Loading a HuggingFace model for the first time produces a substantial amount of terminal noise: download progress bars, LOAD REPORT diagnostics from the model class, deprecation warnings from transformers internals, and unauthenticated-request warnings from the hf_xet Rust extension. In a CLI tool this noise obscures the actual pipeline output.

The suppression strategy is layered:

  1. Environment variables. HF_HUB_DISABLE_PROGRESS_BARS=1 and TRANSFORMERS_VERBOSITY=error before any HuggingFace imports.
  2. Python logging. huggingface_hub, transformers, accelerate, and peft loggers set to ERROR.
  3. Warnings filter. warnings.filterwarnings('ignore') for known deprecation categories.
  4. stdout/stderr redirection. contextlib.redirect_stdout/stderr into a StringIO buffer during model loading, surfaced only if loading fails.
  5. Offline mode. When the base model is already in the HuggingFace cache, HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1 and TRANSFORMERS_OFFLINE=1 are set before loading. This avoids the hf_xet Rust extension's unauthenticated-request warning, which writes directly to file descriptor 2 and bypasses all Python-level redirection.

All suppression is disabled when the user passes --verbose.

docs.title: Advantages
docs.text:
Scalable filtering. The pipeline can process thousands of papers per hour on a laptop CPU, narrowing the full OpenAlex chemistry index down to a short list of plausible dataset releases. This makes the expensive agent workflow (ADR 005) practical at scale — instead of running the agent on every paper, it only runs on the few hundred flagged by the classifier.

Composable workflow. The two-step and single-pass patterns serve different use cases without code duplication. The shared FetchState, build_csv_row, and classifier infrastructure is reused across commands. The file-based hand-off to the agent pipeline requires no coupling between the two systems.

Offline-capable. After the initial model download (model-download), the entire pipeline runs without network access to HuggingFace. Only the OpenAlex API requires connectivity, and even that is resumable across network interruptions.

Accessible. CPU-first design with no mandatory GPU dependency means the pipeline runs on any developer machine, CI runner, or cloud instance. Optional quantization provides a performance boost when hardware is available without making it a requirement.

Inspectable state. Plain-text sidecar files make it trivial to audit, debug, and manually repair pipeline state. No database tooling, no binary formats, no recovery procedures.

docs.title: Disadvantages
docs.text:
Base model download. The TinyLlama-1.1B base model (~2 GB) is downloaded from HuggingFace Hub on first use. This is a one-time cost cached by the Hub, but it can be surprising for users who expected only the ~13 MB adapter download. The model-info command helps diagnose this, and the offline mode detection avoids repeated download checks.

Noise suppression fragility. The layered suppression strategy works today but is coupled to implementation details of HuggingFace libraries (logger names, warning categories, the hf_xet Rust extension's behavior). Library upgrades may introduce new noise sources that require additional suppression layers. The --verbose flag provides an escape hatch when suppression hides a genuine error.

Threshold sensitivity. The default threshold of 0.05 was tuned on the upstream training corpus. On a different distribution of papers (e.g., a subfield with unusual terminology for dataset releases) the recall/precision trade-off may shift. Users can adjust via --threshold but have no built-in way to evaluate the classifier on their own labeled data.

Two command patterns. Having both fetch+score and stream for the same underlying operation adds surface area to the CLI. Users must understand when to use which. The help text and group-level documentation mitigate this, but it is still more to learn than a single command.

Dev extras scope. Placing ML dependencies in [dev] alongside development tools (pytest, ruff, etc.) means a user who only wants to run the discovery pipeline also installs testing infrastructure. A dedicated [discovery] extras group would be more precise but would add yet another extras key to maintain.

docs.title: 009 — Recording a licence on each dataset
docs.text: Status: accepted Date: 2026-08-19 Decided by: the maintainer

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
ChemMatData redistributes other people's data, and until now carried no record of the terms it does so under. metadata.yml had thirteen fields — category, compounds, description, full, min_version, notes, raw, sources, tags, target_descriptions, target_type, targets, verbose — and none of them was a licence.

That was tolerable while licences were established informally. It stopped being tolerable when the extraction pipeline (ADR 005) began systematically establishing a licence for every dataset it produces: stage 1 researches the terms, records them in the run manifest, and blocks on anything non-permissive until a human decides. The conclusion then went no further. A maintainer could accept a ShareAlike obligation on the project's behalf and the person who downloaded the dataset would never learn of it.

The immediate trigger was ChEMBL. Ten datasets in the collection derive their structures from it, and ChEMBL is CC BY-SA 3.0 — attribution and ShareAlike. The attribution half was added on 2026-08-18. The ShareAlike half is an obligation that propagates to downstream users, and there was nowhere to put it. The full analysis is in ../chembl_licensing_analysis.md.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Add an optional license field to dataset metadata, shaped as a mapping:

license:
    identifier: CC-BY-SA-3.0
    url: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/
    note: >
        The molecular structures derive from ChEMBL, which is licensed CC BY-SA 3.0.
        The ShareAlike condition propagates, so this dataset is distributed under the
        same licence.

A mapping rather than a bare SPDX string, for two reasons. First, provenance is usually the interesting part: "CC-BY-SA-3.0" alone does not say why, and the why is what a user needs in order to reason about their own obligations. Second, some datasets cannot be described by an identifier alone — esnuel_mca and esnuel_maa carry a ShareAlike obligation inherited from ChEMBL while their own upstream archive states no terms at all, and a bare identifier would assert a grant that was never made.

The field is optional and its absence means "not established". Most of the collection predates any licence research. An absent license is not a claim that the data is freely usable, and nothing should read it that way.

docs.title: Applied now
docs.text:
The twelve ChEMBL-derived datasets are labelled CC-BY-SA-3.0: dud_e, riniker_1, riniker_1_filtered, riniker_2, bl_chembl_reg, bl_chembl_cls, lipophilicity, dpp4, moleculeace, pparg_binding, esnuel_mca, esnuel_maa.

The rest of the collection is untouched. Licences will be filled in as datasets are touched, and automatically for anything the extraction pipeline produces from now on.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
Users of the twelve inherit a reciprocal obligation. Someone building on lipophilicity or esnuel_mca must offer their derivative under CC-BY-SA-3.0 or a compatible licence. This is a real restriction the project is now placing on its users, deliberately, because it is the obligation ChEMBL attached to the data in the first place. Note it is not a restriction on commercial use — ChEMBL is explicit that ShareAlike does not preclude it.

Scope is bounded by the licence text itself. CC BY-SA 3.0 §4(a) and §4(b) both end by stating that the obligation does not extend to "the Collection apart from the Work/Adaptation itself". The obligation attaches to the individual dataset. It does not reach the catalogue, the other datasets, or the chem_mat_data package.

Three code paths had to learn about the field, all of which enumerate metadata keys explicitly and would otherwise have dropped it:

  • chem_mat_data/cli.py — cmdata info renders a License section, placed before Targets because whether a reader may use the dataset is more urgent than what is in it. Without this the label would exist only in a YAML file nobody reads.
  • chem_mat_data/manage.py — the field list in docs_compile_command.
  • chem_mat_data/agent/gates.py — the metadata gate warns when a draft carries no licence; the verification gate errors when a draft declares one and the shipped metadata.yml does not. The asymmetry is deliberate: forgetting to research a licence is a warning, but establishing one and failing to ship it defeats the entire point.

What this does not settle. Whether ShareAlike legally attaches to a filtered, re-encoded dataset of computed properties is genuinely uncertain — facts are not copyrightable, the protected element would be ChEMBL's selection, and CC BY-SA 3.0 Unported does not mention database rights at all (verified: zero occurrences of "database" or "sui generis" in the legal code). This decision does not resolve that question; it takes the conservative side of it. Asking EMBL-EBI directly would settle it, and remains worth doing.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text:
A bare license: CC-BY-SA-3.0 string. Simpler and easier to filter on, but cannot express inheritance or an unstated upstream without asserting something false.

Attribute without propagating — credit ChEMBL, decline to pass the obligation on. This is what DeepChem/MoleculeNet, TDC and OGB effectively do. Rejected as a legal judgement the project would be making without counsel; the conservative option costs users a licence label, the permissive one costs them a defence.

Licence every dataset now. Rejected as disproportionate: most have never had their licence researched, so it would mean either weeks of work or a great many honest "unknown" entries that add nothing.

docs.title: Licence determination — tmQMg-L
docs.text:
Verdict: ESCALATE TO HUMAN. Two independent reasons, either of which is sufficient under references/license.md:

  1. The data licence is CC-BY-NC-4.0 — a NonCommercial variant, explicitly in the ESCALATE column of the policy table.
  2. The data is derived from the Cambridge Structural Database (CSD), a commercial licensed database whose operator (CCDC) states in writing that CSD data may not be redistributed and that external distribution of derived datasets requires a separate signed agreement.

There is no charitable reading available here. Both findings point the same way.

  • LICENSE file: https://github.com/uiocompcat/tmQMg-L/blob/main/LICENSE

I checked the body: it contains the NonCommercial means not primarily intended for or directed towards commercial advantage or monetary compensation definition (line 116), and Section 2 grants only reproduce and Share the Licensed Material, in whole or in part, for NonCommercial purposes only and produce, reproduce, and Share Adapted Material for NonCommercial purposes only (lines 152–155). Greps for ShareAlike and NoDerivatives return zero hits, so this is plain BY-NC, not BY-NC-SA and not BY-NC-ND.
  • README licence notice (bottom of https://github.com/uiocompcat/tmQMg-L#readme), verbatim:

This is not evidence of an unclear licence — CC BY-NC 4.0 simply is not in GitHub's licensee picklist, so any repo using it detects as "Other". The LICENSE file text itself is unambiguous.
